variety: Over 20,000 roses, 2,000+ varieties
tip: Visit early morning when the dew is still on the petals. The fragrance is strongest before 9am.
story: Few gardens in India hold this kind of scale. Ooty's rose garden spreads across terraced hillsides — over twenty thousand plants, more than two thousand varieties, all perched at seven thousand feet above sea level. The mornings here are cool in a way only these hills can manage, and the roses hold onto the dew like small held breaths. Go before nine, when the fragrance is strongest and the gardeners haven't yet started their rounds. You smell them before you see them. There are Damasks the color of old photographs, climbers twisted around wooden arches, deep red hybrid teas that look almost black at sunrise. Wear a cardigan and walk slowly, bending now and then to read the little metal name tags. The garden is easy to reach: a morning train from Coimbatore, a flask of hot chai at the gate, and the whole afternoon to wander. No hurry, no plan, just the long rows and the smell of everything opening at once.

variety: Sweet almond (Prunus dulcis)
tip: The road from Santiago del Teide to Arguayo is the best driving route through the blossoms.
story: On the high slopes of Tenerife, winter does something unusual — it throws flowers instead of snow. For a few weeks in late January and February, the almond orchards above Santiago del Teide come into bloom, and the pale pink clouds float against a volcano that's still sometimes capped in white. The drive from Santiago del Teide to Arguayo is the one to take — slow and winding, windows down, the air full of soft almond perfume. Locals call this the almendros en flor season, and they've marked it with a festival for generations, a celebration of light returning. The bloom is fleeting — miss it by a week and the blossoms are gone, replaced by green leaves and the beginning of fruit. It's the kind of bloom that teaches you to show up on time. Stop at any of the little pueblos along the way for a bowl of almond soup and a piece of bienmesabe — the Canarian almond dessert — and watch the orchards stretch toward the sea.

variety: Taiwan Cherry (Prunus campanulata)
tip: Take the bus from Shilin MRT to avoid traffic. The mountain gets jammed on weekends.
story: Yangmingshan sits right above Taipei — you can be in the city's noise in the morning and standing under pale pink cherry trees by lunchtime. The Taiwan cherry blooms earlier than its Japanese cousins, in a deeper, almost magenta shade that looks like watercolor against the mountain mist. Take the bus from Shilin MRT; the mountain road jams with cars on weekends, and the bus lets you look out the windows. The park has hot springs too, so after the flowers you can soak your feet in water that smells faintly of sulfur and earth. There's something Taipei does casually — a city of seven million, and just twenty minutes up the road are silent hillsides covered in blossom, with cups of oolong being poured in wooden teahouses. Go on a weekday if you can. Find one of the benches under the trees, close your eyes, and listen to the little birds they call white-eyes moving through the branches.

variety: Nymphaea nouchali (national flower)
tip: Rent a bicycle and ride the wetland trail at sunrise.
story: The Maldives are known for beaches, but tucked into the southernmost atoll is something quieter — Hithadhoo's freshwater wetlands, where the national flower blooms across still water. The Nymphaea nouchali is small, star-shaped, purple at the center fading to pale lavender, and it opens with the sun. The wetlands are ribboned with walking paths and wooden boardwalks that let you get close without disturbing anything. Rent a bicycle in the village and ride the loop at sunrise — the light comes in low across the water, the lilies lift their heads, and you hear the place wake up around you, birds and frogs and a breeze through the palm trees. This is the part of the Maldives the brochures skip, and it's somehow the part that stays with you. Take a thermos of tea. Stop on one of the benches. Watch the lilies open one by one, the way a book opens its pages.

variety: Handroanthus chrysotrichus (Golden Trumpet Tree)
tip: The trees along Avenida Atlântica in Copacabana are the most photogenic.
story: There's a moment in Rio's summer when the city turns yellow. The ipê amarelo — the golden trumpet tree — flowers almost all at once, and suddenly the avenues of Copacabana, the hills above Santa Teresa, the quiet streets of Laranjeiras, all become lit from above by canopies of gold. The trees shed their leaves before blooming, so the flowers look like they're floating unattached. Avenida Atlântica is the most photographed stretch, with the sea on one side and the golden tunnel on the other. The smaller streets reward attention too — Rua Jardim Botânico, the paths inside the botanical gardens themselves — where you can hear a bird and smell the coffee from a corner café. The ipê is Brazil's national tree, and Brazilians mark its blooming the way other places mark a festival. Walk slowly. Look up often. The petals fall in that specific way yellow petals fall, and for a few weeks the sidewalks look like someone has scattered gold all over the city.

variety: Rapeseed / Canola
tip: The Golden Rooster Hill viewpoint gives the best panoramic view of the golden sea.
story: In February, one corner of Yunnan turns completely gold. The Luoping plateau grows canola — rapeseed — across hundreds of thousands of acres, and when it flowers, the hills between the karst mountains look like a sea that someone has painted yellow. Climb to the Golden Rooster Hill viewpoint at dawn. The mist rolls between the limestone peaks and the fields below, and the sun catches the flowers and sets everything alight. The local Miao and Buyi farmers have grown rapeseed here for generations; the honey that comes from these fields is some of the best in China, thick and pale and tasting faintly of the flowers themselves. Buy a jar at one of the roadside stalls. Stay for two days if you can — the light changes hour by hour. Wake early, take a long breakfast of rice noodles at one of the small shops, then ride a bike into the fields. The canola is not a showy flower up close, just four small yellow petals, but multiplied by millions it becomes one of the quieter wonders on Earth.

variety: 5 million almond trees turn pink
tip: Drive the road from Valldemossa to Sóller for the most concentrated blossoms against mountain backdrops.
story: Five million almond trees grow on Mallorca, and in early February they all bloom at once. The island becomes another version of itself — the stone villages half-hidden in pink, the terraced hillsides going pale against the mountains. The drive from Valldemossa to Sóller is the one to make slowly, with frequent stops at lay-bys and small cafés. You'll find yourself pulling over just to stand in an orchard for a few minutes, the white-pink petals dropping onto your shoulders. The almond was brought here by the Moors a thousand years ago, and the trees still follow the old irrigation terraces they built. Try an ensaïmada dusted with icing sugar at a village bakery — the island's traditional almond-and-honey pastries during this season taste like the air. The blossoms only hold for two or three weeks. Come early on a weekday, follow the small roads inland, and let the island show you what February can look like when it decides to be gentle.

variety: Kawazu-zakura (blooms a month before Somei Yoshino)
tip: Walk along the Kawazu River where 8,000 trees line both banks for 4km.
story: Most people think cherry blossoms mean April, but Kawazu on the Izu Peninsula doesn't wait. Its cherry — the Kawazu-zakura — blooms a whole month early, in mid-February, when the rest of Japan is still in winter coats. The variety has bigger, deeper-pink petals than the famous Somei Yoshino, and they hang on the trees for almost a month instead of a week. Eight thousand trees line both banks of the Kawazu River for four kilometers; you walk the path at dusk with lanterns glowing pink overhead and the river running quiet below. The town holds a festival for the whole season — food stalls along the river selling grilled squid and sweet bean dumplings, little carts of hot amazake to warm your hands. Take the train from Tokyo in the morning, spend the afternoon walking both banks, and sit for a long dinner of fresh fish at one of the ryokan inns. It's the country's first hanami of the year, and it feels like a secret.

variety: Prunus cerasoides
tip: The cherry trees near Xuan Huong Lake are the easiest to find.
story: Da Lat sits in the cool mountains of Vietnam's central highlands, and every January and February its wild Himalayan cherries — Prunus cerasoides — cover the hills in pale pink. The French built this city as a retreat from the heat of Saigon, and you can still feel that softness: mist in the pine trees, cafés that serve strawberry jam and tart yellow coffee, old villas with rose gardens. The easiest cherry trees to find are the ones near Xuan Huong Lake, right in the center of town — you can walk the whole loop in an hour, with blossoms on one side and paddle boats on the other. Stop at a market stall for an artichoke tea or a warm cup of sữa đậu nành. The mornings are crisp here, almost cold, and the afternoons get soft with sun. Stay at one of the little guesthouses in the French quarter, and wake early for the cherries before the day warms up. Da Lat is Vietnam's flower capital — you'll see roses, mimosa, and hydrangeas everywhere — but it's the cherry trees that make January feel like a gift.

variety: Multiple varieties — white, pink, yellow, red
tip: Kula Botanical Garden has the most diverse collection on Maui.
story: On Maui, plumeria grows like it's been waiting for you. You'll find it at the side of the road, spilling over garden walls, dropped onto the sidewalks by children — white, yellow, deep pink, sometimes all three on the same tree. The smell is like nothing else: sweet but not heavy, a little peppery, the kind of fragrance you catch on a breeze and try to find again. Kula Botanical Garden, up in the cool hills, has the most diverse plumeria collection on the island, with varieties brought from all over the Pacific. Take a slow drive up there in the morning when the air is still cool, and plan to spend an hour just walking between trees. In Hawaii, plumeria is the flower of welcome. Women tuck it behind one ear when they're single, behind the other when they're spoken for. Buy a lei from one of the stands near the airport — not the plastic kind, the fresh one that smells like the whole island — and wear it all day.

variety: Dahlia (Mexico's national flower), 42 species
tip: Visit during the Night That Nobody Sleeps festival in August for dahlia-covered floats.
story: The dahlia is Mexico's national flower, and Huamantla is where it lives best. In spring the fields and gardens around this small Tlaxcala town come into bloom in every color you can imagine — the pom-pom ones, the dinner-plate ones, the little star-shaped singles — and the local nurseries open their gates to visitors. The Aztec word for dahlia was acocoxochitl, and they ate the tubers long before Europeans knew the flower existed. If you can come back in August, Huamantla has one of the country's most beautiful festivals — La Noche Que Nadie Duerme, the Night That Nobody Sleeps — where the streets are carpeted with flowers and sawdust in elaborate designs, and floats covered in dahlias roll through the town at midnight. The bakeries here sell a bread called muéganos, crunchy and sweet and coated in sugar, perfect with a cup of hot chocolate while you watch the afternoon light come down on the fields. It's a small town, proud of its flowers, and it welcomes anyone who comes for them.

variety: Maehwa (Korean plum blossom)
tip: The Seomjin River trail through the village is the most scenic walk.
story: While the rest of Korea is still thinking about the cold, Gwangyang is already in blossom. The village sits on a hillside above the Seomjin River, and in late February and early March its hundred thousand plum trees — maehwa — break out in white flowers that smell like honey and almond. Walk the river trail through the village and stop at one of the tea houses serving plum tea and maesil jam on warm bread. Korean plum blossom is a symbol of strength — it flowers before the winter has fully let go, sometimes through a last snowfall. The village has been growing plums for over a hundred years, and there's a festival every year with traditional music and plates of pork belly eaten with plum sauce. Go on a weekday, early in the morning, when the mist is still in the valley and the river is pink with reflected flowers. Stay for lunch. Buy a jar of plum syrup to take home. The season is short — two weeks at most — but the village stays warm in memory long after.

variety: Plumeria rubra, alba
tip: The oldest botanic garden in Africa. Visit the orchid house too.
story: Durban Botanic Gardens is the oldest surviving botanic garden in Africa, founded in 1849, and the frangipani trees inside have been blooming every summer for more than a century. The flowers are creamy white with yellow throats, the classic five petals arranged like a little pinwheel, and they drop to the paths in soft piles that release their perfume underfoot. Walk the Sunken Garden loop in the early morning — the gardens open at 7:30 — and loop back through the orchid house and the cycad collection, some of which are older than the trees themselves. A small café near the entrance does a proper South African breakfast, eggs and chakalaka and a good cup of rooibos. Durban has a deep Indian community too, and you'll find it in the food and gardens everywhere — jasmine and curry leaf, hibiscus and bougainvillea. The frangipani is a tropical flower that has adopted this coast like it was always meant to be here. Sit a while under the big trees, close your eyes, and let the perfume do its work.

variety: Darwin Hybrids, Triumph, Parrot
tip: Go on a weekday morning before 10am. The fields on Beaver Marsh Road are less crowded.
story:
Skagit Valley is an hour north of Seattle, a flat patchwork of farmland wedged between the Cascade mountains and the Salish Sea. Every April it turns into ribbons of color — whole fields of red, yellow, purple, orange, row after perfect row, stretching for miles. The farmers here have been growing bulbs for four generations, descended from Dutch immigrants who arrived in the early 1900s. The valley now ships tulip bulbs all over the world.

Go on a weekday morning if you can — the weekends fill quickly. Beaver Marsh Road lets you walk the field edges without the crowds. Tulip Town and RoozenGaarde are the two main farms with proper visitor experiences, gift shops, and demonstration gardens. The Skagit Valley Tulip Festival runs the entire month of April, with bloom timing announced fresh each year on the festival's website — the Pacific Northwest weather can shift the peak by a week or two.

Bring a thermos of something warm. April mornings here can still surprise you with cold mist, and then the sun breaks through and the whole valley lights up. Stop at one of the small farm stands for cardamom tea and a slice of apple pie. The Cascade peaks watch over the fields in the distance, and the tulips in the foreground feel almost too vivid to be real.

variety: Yoshino (Somei Yoshino) — 3,000 trees
tip: Paddle a boat on the Tidal Basin at golden hour. The reflections of cherry blossoms in the water are extraordinary.
story: Washington's cherry trees were a gift from Tokyo to the United States in 1912, three thousand Somei Yoshino carried across the Pacific by ship. They still bloom every spring around the Tidal Basin, under the same sky where they were first planted. At peak, the whole basin becomes a pale pink horizon — you walk the two-mile loop and the blossoms meet over your head the whole way. The best thing to do is rent a paddle boat and go out on the water at golden hour. The Jefferson Memorial sits white and solemn across the basin, and the cherry trees lean out over the water, and everything reflects — stone, petals, slow current, the small birds and the people on the paths. Come early — seven in the morning if you can — or late, when the light softens and the crowds thin. The trees only hold their flowers for about two weeks, and you'll want every hour of it. Bring a thermos of something warm. Washington in early spring can still surprise you with a cold morning.

variety: Eschscholzia californica (state flower)
tip: The south-facing hillsides bloom first. Follow the 7-mile Antelope Loop Trail.
story: In a good year the Antelope Valley turns into a sea of orange. California poppies — the state flower — cover whole hillsides by the millions, and from the top of the seven-mile Antelope Loop Trail you can see the poppies rippling in the wind like a living coat. The reserve is about an hour and a half north of Los Angeles, in the western Mojave Desert, and the weather there is cool in March and April, often windy, sometimes misty at dawn. The south-facing slopes bloom first. Walk slowly — poppies close up at midday heat and in the wind, so catch them in the early morning or late afternoon when the petals are fully open and the low sun is lighting them from within. Pack water and a hat. The reserve has no food, so bring a sandwich and eat it on one of the benches looking out over Antelope Buttes. Some years the bloom is modest; other years it's the kind of landscape you think only happens in paintings. Check the daily bloom report before you go.

variety: Giant Tecolote Ranunculus — 50 acres of color
tip: Go to the top of the hill for the view of flowers meeting the ocean.
story: Fifty acres of ranunculus sit on a hill above the Pacific in Carlsbad, California — a ribboned patchwork of red, yellow, pink, orange, white, and apricot that's been coming back every March for nearly a hundred years. The Tecolote ranunculus was developed here by a family that bred it from wild Asian varieties, and you won't see this scale of the flower anywhere else on Earth. Walk to the top of the hill — the view from there is what you want: endless color stepping down toward the ocean. A small train takes you around the perimeter if the paths get hot. Go on a weekday morning, buy a cup of coffee and a lemon scone at the little stand near the entrance, and take the path that leads into the rose garden tucked inside the larger field. Ranunculus don't have fragrance, which surprised me the first time — they're all color. But the color! Rows and rows of tight, papery layers, each flower looking like something folded by hand. Stay for the sunset. The light from the ocean turns everything gold, even the flowers that are already gold.

variety: 7 million bulbs, 800+ varieties
tip: Book the earliest entry slot. The Juliana pavilion in the back has the rarest varieties and no crowds.
story: Keukenhof is the largest spring garden in the world — seven million bulbs planted by hand each autumn, eight hundred varieties, thirty-two hectares of designed beauty. The gardens open for only eight weeks a year, March to May, and then they close again for the bulbs to rest. Book the earliest entry slot. The park empties out at lunch when tour buses pull away, but if you're inside at 8am you'll have the first hours to yourself. The Juliana pavilion at the back holds the rarest varieties — historical tulips from the Ottoman Empire, delicate species tulips, the famous striped Rembrandts that once caused a financial bubble in 17th-century Holland. Rent a bicycle and take the Bollenstreek route through the surrounding fields — commercial tulip farms where the color is shocking, unsubtle, endless. Buy raw herring from a stall, or a cone of hot stroopwafels. The Dutch love this season like no other country loves anything, and you can feel it in every small pleasure they offer you here. Bring a light rain jacket. The Netherlands is generous with its flowers and its weather.

variety: Dutch hyacinths — fragrant striped fields
tip: Rent a bike from Leiden and cycle through the Bollenstreek flower route.
story: The Bollenstreek — the Dutch bulb region — is mostly known for its tulips, but in March and early April it belongs to the hyacinths. The fields around Lisse turn into striped bands of deep purple, pale blue, pink, and white, and the smell — oh, the smell. Hyacinth fragrance is heavy and sweet and drifts for miles on the wind; you smell the fields before you see them. Rent a bicycle from Leiden in the morning and cycle the flower route north — it's flat, well-signed, and passes farm after farm, each with a little stand selling flowers by the bunch. Stop for coffee and apple cake at one of the village cafés. The Dutch call this time bollenseizoen, bulb season, and they take it seriously — every farmhouse has a bouquet in the window, every window box is full. Hyacinths only last a few weeks before they're cut down to let the bulbs grow for next year, so come early in the season when the fields are at their full height. The color of an entire field of hyacinths is a color you don't forget.

variety: 350,000 cherry trees — largest cherry blossom festival in the world
tip: Walk along the Yeojwacheon Stream — cherry blossoms form a tunnel over the water.
story: Jinhae is a small port city in southeastern Korea, and every April it becomes the site of the largest cherry blossom festival in the world. Three hundred and fifty thousand trees line the streets, parks, and waterways, and for ten days the whole town turns pale pink. The heart of the festival is the Yeojwacheon Stream, where the cherry trees have grown across the water and formed a tunnel of blossoms so complete that you walk under a pink ceiling for the length of the canal. Come at dusk when the lanterns light up — the stream becomes one of the most photographed places in Asia. Walk also to the Gyeonghwa train station, where a short stretch of disused track runs between tight rows of cherry trees. The town's coffee shops sell cherry-blossom lattes that are more pink than pink has any right to be. Korean families come for picnics, couples in matching jackets pose beneath the trees, old men in flat caps drink makgeolli from paper cups. It's loud, and busy, and joyful, and impossible not to feel pulled into by the end of an afternoon.

variety: Rosa damascena (Damask Rose)
tip: Time your visit for the Rose Festival in May. The entire town smells like rosewater.
story: In the Dadès Valley, high between the Atlas Mountains and the Sahara, one town grows the world's most perfumed roses. Kelaat M'Gouna has been cultivating the Damask rose for five hundred years, since the petals were first brought back by pilgrims returning from Mecca. Every May, the valley holds a three-day festival — Moussem of the Roses — and the whole region comes alive with music, processions, and the smell of rosewater being distilled in copper stills. Buy a small bottle at one of the cooperatives. The local Berber women gather the flowers before sunrise when the petal oil is at its highest — if you wake early, you can join a harvest, tie a cloth around your waist, and fill a basket in the pink morning air. The gardens are long hedges, kilometers of them, following the irrigation channels between fields of wheat and alfalfa. After the festival, stop at a village café for a glass of rose-flavored tea and sweet almond pastries. The drive back to Marrakech takes you over the High Atlas — the roses travel with you in the car, in your clothes, on your skin.

variety: Japanese Wisteria — including a 150-year-old Great Wisteria tree
tip: Go at night during the illumination event. The purple cascades lit up are otherworldly.
story: Ashikaga Flower Park is built around a single tree — a 150-year-old wisteria so vast that wooden supports hold up its branches like an enormous trellis, and the purple flowers cascade down in waterfalls you can walk under. The tree covers nearly 2,000 square meters, and during the illumination event at night it's lit from below in soft purple and white. The park also has tunnels of white wisteria, pale yellow laburnum, and a corridor of pink azaleas, so your walk through the gardens keeps changing color. Go in the evening. The crowds thin after sunset, and the lights come on — the big tree becomes something from a dream, almost moving in the breeze. The fragrance of wisteria is delicate, sweet, a little grape-like. Stop at the food stalls for takoyaki or grilled mochi. The train from Tokyo takes about two hours — it's a day trip if you start early, or stay overnight at one of the nearby ryokan and see the park both in daylight and at night. No photograph quite captures it. The tree has to be stood under.

variety: Lupinus texensis (Texas state flower)
tip: Highway 290 between Fredericksburg and Johnson City has the densest patches.
story: For a few weeks in late March and early April, the Texas Hill Country turns a color that Texans will argue about forever — the bluebonnet blue, a deep violet-blue that's neither quite blue nor quite purple, but is entirely, undeniably, Texas. The Lupinus texensis is the state flower, and it grows in wide drifts along the shoulders of Highway 290 between Fredericksburg and Johnson City, in pastures and along fence lines and across whole hillsides. Drive the back roads slowly. Pull over where other cars have pulled over — that's the local etiquette — and walk carefully into a patch for a photograph. Texans have a long tradition of photographing their babies in bluebonnets, and you'll see families doing this, kids in small cowboy hats sitting very seriously in the flowers. Fredericksburg is the town to base in: German heritage, small bakeries selling apple strudel, a long main street of peach orchards and wineries. Come for a weekend, go wildflower hunting in the morning, eat brisket for lunch, and end the day at one of the small wineries with a view over the hills still blooming.

variety: 4.5 million baby blue eyes covering rolling hills
tip: Arrive right at opening (9:30am). By 11am it's packed. The west hill is less crowded than the main Miharashi Hill.
story: Four and a half million baby blue eyes cover the rolling hills of Hitachi Seaside Park. Nemophila menziesii is a small blue flower — five pale-blue petals with a white eye at the center — and by itself it looks modest, even shy. But multiplied across 4.5 hectares of Miharashi Hill, the effect is surreal. The hills seem to merge with the sky. When you climb to the top, there's a moment when you can't quite tell where the blue of the flowers ends and the blue of the ocean and sky begin. The Japanese have a word for this — aozora, blue sky — and this is what that feels like in solid form. Arrive at the opening bell, 9:30 am. By 11 the park fills with tour buses. The west hill is less crowded than Miharashi but just as beautiful. Stop for ice cream at the little kiosk halfway up. Rent a bicycle for the longer loop through tulip beds, poppies, and coastal trails. The train from Tokyo takes about an hour and a half. Come on a clear day — the blue needs the blue of the sky to be complete.

variety: 800,000 moss phlox in pink, white, magenta
tip: Visit at sunrise for the clearest view of Fuji. Afternoon haze often hides the mountain.
story: At the foot of Mount Fuji, 800,000 pink moss plants cover the ground in a 2.4-hectare ribbon of color that stretches toward the mountain. Shibazakura — literally 'lawn cherry' — isn't a cherry at all but a low ground-cover phlox that grows in pink, white, magenta, and pale lilac. The effect against Fuji is something that feels designed by a careful hand. Go at sunrise. Fuji almost always hides behind afternoon haze, but the early morning is when it stands completely clean against the sky, and the low light makes the flowers glow. A café at the site sells Fuji-shaped steamed buns and hot tea, which you need because the morning air up at Lake Motosu can be cold even in May. The festival runs from mid-April to late May. If you have a car, combine it with a visit to the other Five Lakes — Kawaguchi has the best reflection of Fuji, Saiko has hot springs, Yamanaka is quieter. But the pink moss festival is the centerpiece. A field of soft pink with the white cone of Fuji above it — it's an image that stays with you.

variety: 30 million tulips planted across the city each year
tip: Emirgan Park is the main festival venue but Gülhane Park near Topkapı Palace is more intimate.
story: Tulips are not originally Dutch. They're from the Ottoman Empire, and Istanbul is where they first became an obsession — painted on tiles at Topkapı Palace, embroidered on robes, celebrated in poetry, and planted in vast numbers across the royal gardens. Every April, the city plants thirty million tulips across parks, medians, and roundabouts. Emirgan Park on the European side of the Bosphorus is the festival's main site — sweeping lawns that descend toward the water, tulips planted in dense curves of color, pavilions where Ottoman-era music is played on ney and kanun. For something more intimate, Gülhane Park next to Topkapı Palace is smaller and less crowded, with cats dozing between the flower beds and views across the Golden Horn. Stop at a pastane afterward for baklava and a glass of çay. The Turkish word for tulip, lâle, shares its letters with the word for Allah — the flower became a symbol of the divine during the Tulip Era of the 1700s, when whole festivals were held under lantern-lit tulip beds. Istanbul returned the flower to Holland, and now, after four centuries, it's returned again to itself.

variety: Hyacinthoides non-scripta — purple carpet under beech trees
tip: Follow the marked walking trail — leaving the path damages the flowers and is prohibited.
story: Hallerbos is a small beech forest south of Brussels, and for about three weeks in April its floor turns completely purple. Wild bluebells — Hyacinthoides non-scripta — come up by the millions through last year's leaves, and because the beech canopy hasn't yet leafed out, the sunlight falls straight down through the bare branches onto this layer of intense, saturated color. It looks like someone has laid a purple carpet through the whole forest. The park has marked walking trails and asks you to stay on them — trampling the bluebells damages next year's bloom. Follow the main loop, which takes you through the densest patches, and if you have time add the longer trail through the younger forest where the flowers mix with wild anemones and yellow wood-sorrel. Go on a weekday. The weekends, especially in peak, draw crowds from all over Belgium and the Netherlands. Bring a camera — the light at mid-morning, filtered through the bare beech branches, is the best you'll get anywhere. The forest has no café, so pack a small picnic and eat somewhere quiet under the trees, the bluebells reaching up around your feet.

variety: 6 million tulips across the city
tip: Veldheer Tulip Gardens is the best spot for photos. Windmill Island has the DeZwaan windmill from the Netherlands.
story: Holland is a small city in western Michigan founded by Dutch immigrants in 1847, and it takes the Dutch tulip tradition seriously. Six million tulips bloom across the town every May — in public parks, along streets, around the DeZwaan windmill that was shipped over from the Netherlands in 1964 and is the only authentic working windmill in the United States. The annual Tulip Time Festival includes Dutch dances, klompen wooden-shoe parades, and fresh stroopwafels sold out of little carts. Veldheer Tulip Gardens has the best organized displays — 30 acres with six million tulips arranged by color and variety — and Windmill Island Gardens, where the DeZwaan turns, gives you the full Dutch village experience. The lakes here are still cold in May, but the tulips don't mind. Base yourself in downtown Holland at one of the small inns, walk the paved flower path along the lakeshore, and eat a proper Dutch breakfast of bread, cheese, and coffee at the Wooden Shoe diner. It's a postcard-small town, but it does this season with a joy that feels fully earned.

variety: Over 1 million peonies, 1,200+ varieties
tip: Luoyang has celebrated the peony for over 1,500 years. The city literally shuts down during peak bloom.
story: Luoyang has loved peonies for 1,500 years. When the Tang Dynasty empress Wu Zetian banished peonies from her capital in the 7th century, the flower took refuge in Luoyang, and it has stayed here ever since. More than a million peonies bloom across the city each April — over a thousand varieties, from giant tree peonies to delicate herbaceous ones, in colors that run from white to almost-black. The National Peony Garden is the largest single collection, but the whole city participates. During the Peony Festival, streets are closed, lanterns hung, and poetry is read in the gardens under the blooming trees. The peony is often called the king of flowers in China, and when you see a tree peony the size of a dinner plate, you understand. Walk the garden slowly. Each named variety has its own small placard in Chinese and English. Stop for lunch at one of the Luoyang water banquets — a 24-course meal of broths and stews that goes back to the Tang. Stay overnight and come back to the gardens in the morning, when the dew is still on the petals and the crowds haven't yet arrived.

variety: 1,700+ species — orchids, poppies, anemones, cyclamens
tip: The Samaria Gorge trail in spring is carpeted with wildflowers. The Omalos Plateau is easier to access.
story: Crete is one of the wildflower capitals of Europe. More than 1,700 species grow on this island, and about 160 of them are endemic — they grow nowhere else. In April, the Samaria Gorge and the Omalos Plateau become tapestries of orchids, wild tulips, poppies, cyclamens, anemones, and crocuses. Some of these flowers were sacred to the Minoans 4,000 years ago — you can find them painted on the walls of Knossos. The Samaria Gorge hike is a long one, sixteen kilometers through pine forest and rock walls, with flowers at your feet the whole way. If that's too much, the Omalos Plateau sits at 1,000 meters elevation and has gentle meadow walks that are carpeted in flowers. Stop for a lunch of stuffed vine leaves and fresh cheese at a mountain taverna. Order a glass of raki. Crete in spring is mild and green, nothing like the hot dry island of the summer postcards — there's water in the streams, white blossoms on the almond trees, and the occasional cold wind off the White Mountains. Bring a small flower guide. You'll want to know their names.

variety: 46 species of rhododendron — national flower of Bhutan
tip: The trek from Paro to the Tiger's Nest monastery passes through blooming rhododendron forests.
story: The rhododendron is Bhutan's national flower, and in spring the Paro Valley and the trail up to Tiger's Nest monastery pass through forests of them in full bloom. Forty-six species grow here — red, pink, white, pale yellow, magenta — some of them tree-sized, some low and shrubby, all of them dense with flowers. The trek up to Tiger's Nest is steep, about three hours, and you climb through rhododendron forests that give way to pine and then to the sheer cliff where the monastery clings. Prayer flags ripple across the valley below. The air is thin; go slowly. Stop at the teahouse halfway for butter tea and a bowl of the red rice cooked with chili and cheese. The Bhutanese call the rhododendron etho metho, and the flowers bloom from lower valleys up the mountains as spring climbs. Come in early April for the valley bloom, later April and May for higher elevations. Bhutan requires a guide and a daily fee, but you will never see another country do slowness so well. Paro is a good place to practice it — walk the valley, visit the monasteries, and let the flowers show you their schedule.

variety: 10,000 rose bushes, 650 varieties
tip: Free admission. Go at sunset — the view of Mt. Hood behind the roses is the best in Portland.
story: Portland calls itself the City of Roses, and the International Rose Test Garden is the reason. Ten thousand rose bushes, six hundred and fifty varieties, the oldest continuously operating public rose test garden in the United States — founded in 1917 as a sanctuary for European roses during World War I. The garden sits on a hillside in Washington Park with a view across downtown Portland to Mount Hood in the distance. Go at sunset. The low light turns the white roses almost golden, and Mount Hood stands pink at the horizon. Admission is free — Portland is generous like that. Wear comfortable shoes; the garden is larger than it looks, with terraces stepping down the hillside. Stop at the Japanese Garden next door afterward for tea and the raked-gravel calm. Portland in June smells like roses the way Kyoto in April smells like cherries. Even the supermarket parking lots have rose bushes. The test garden holds old roses from the Middle Ages and brand-new hybrids being trialed for commercial release. Bring your nose. The modern roses are stunning, but the heritage roses are the ones that make you close your eyes.

variety: Rosa damascena — harvested for rosewater
tip: Visit during the Golab-Giri (rosewater) festival. Watch rose petals being distilled into rosewater in copper pots.
story: Kashan grows roses the way other places grow wheat. The Rosa damascena has been cultivated here for a thousand years, harvested before dawn by women who move through the fields with cloth bags. The flowers are distilled into rosewater in copper stills — golab — and the perfume that comes off a rose farm at harvest time is a thing you can feel in your chest. Come in May for the Golab-Giri festival, when every village in the region is boiling and distilling at once, and the air is heavy with the smell. The town of Kashan is beautiful in its own right — pink-and-blue tiled mosques, traditional merchant houses with courtyards and wind towers, a covered bazaar where you can buy rose jam, rose syrup, rose tea, rose soap. Iranian rosewater is used in everything: saffron ice cream, tea, wedding ceremonies, traditional medicine. Visit one of the cooperative distilleries and watch the process — petals layered into copper, heated slowly, the clear distillate running out into glass bottles. Buy a small jar of rose jam. It will last you months and taste like Persian poetry, which is the only way I can describe it.

variety: Water lilies, irises, wisteria, roses — Monet's living palette
tip: Go on a Tuesday or Thursday morning — weekends are brutal. Walk directly to the water garden first, then loop back to the flower garden.
story: Claude Monet bought this small village house in 1883 and spent the rest of his life making it beautiful. The flower garden in front — the Clos Normand — is a riot of color, with roses over arches, poppies, irises, nasturtiums spilling over paths. Behind it, across a small road, is the water garden, with the Japanese bridge and the famous pond where the water lilies float. He painted these pools for thirty years. You're walking through his palette. Go on a Tuesday or Thursday morning. The weekends are brutal, and the tours from Paris don't arrive until 10:30. Walk directly to the water garden first — cross the little tunnel under the road, come out on the other side, and take your time along the pond. The water lilies bloom from June through September, but the whole garden is something in May — irises everywhere, wisteria on the bridge. The house is open too, painted yellow and blue inside, Monet's Japanese prints on every wall. Have lunch at one of the auberges in the village after. Giverny is tiny, and it keeps its gentle spell the moment you leave the crowd.

variety: World's most famous flower show — curated gardens and exhibits
tip: Go on the last day when exhibitors sell their plants and flowers at steep discounts.
story: The Chelsea Flower Show is the grand dame of the world's garden exhibitions — five days each May in the grounds of the Royal Hospital in London, where the best gardeners on Earth spend months building show gardens only to dismantle them at the end of the week. Every national newspaper covers it. The Queen used to walk through at the official preview, and it's still considered the most prestigious horticultural event anywhere. Go on the last day, Saturday, when exhibitors sell off their plants and flowers in what is politely called the sell-off and much less politely fought over. You can leave with armloads of rare roses, mature shrubs, whole display arrangements, at steep discounts. The Great Pavilion alone — a 12,000-square-meter tent — is worth the entry, with nurseries from every county of the UK showing their best. Tickets sell out months in advance. Wear comfortable shoes. Eat at one of the posh food stalls. And take notes. You'll come away with a garden's worth of ideas and at least one plant you didn't know you wanted but now absolutely need.

variety: 2,500 hectares of commercial tulip fields
tip: Unlike Keukenhof which is a garden, this is working farmland. Rent a bike from Emmeloord and cycle the 100km route.
story: Keukenhof is a garden; Noordoostpolder is farmland. This is the commercial heart of Dutch tulip growing — 2,500 hectares of working bulb fields in geometric ribbons across the reclaimed polder. No show gardens, no arranged displays, just agriculture at its most beautiful. Rent a bike in Emmeloord and follow the signed Tulip Route — 100 kilometers you can do over a day or split across two. The fields are laid out in enormous colored bands, and because the region is so flat and open, you can see them stretching for miles. Come in late April when the bloom is full. Small farmhouses along the way sell coffee and apple cake, and some of them let you walk the field edges. The Dutch word for this landscape is bollenland, bulb land. It was ocean floor a hundred years ago, drained and reclaimed by engineers and farmers. Every April the polder blooms in a way that feels like a gift from the land itself. Stay at a B&B in one of the small villages. Eat herring from a stand. Cycle east at sunset, when the low sun lights up the stripes of color and everything looks painted.

variety: 1.5 million tulips — Asia's largest tulip garden
tip: The garden sits on a hillside overlooking Dal Lake. Walk to the top terrace for the best view.
story: The Indira Gandhi Tulip Garden sits on a hillside overlooking Dal Lake in Srinagar, and at 1.5 million tulips, it's Asia's largest tulip garden. The flowers bloom in April, just as the apple and almond orchards elsewhere in the valley are opening, and the whole Kashmir Valley becomes a soft bowl of color under snow-capped mountains. Walk to the top terrace — the view from there is the Dal Lake below, wooden shikaras sliding across the water, the old Mughal Shalimar Gardens in the distance, and, behind it all, the Pir Panjal range. The Mughals called Kashmir their paradise, and they built garden after garden here. This tulip garden is newer but fits into that long tradition. Take a shikara ride on Dal Lake afterward. Have kahwa — saffron and cinnamon tea with almonds — at one of the floating houseboat restaurants. A few days here pair naturally with the rest of the valley: stay on a houseboat, take long slow walks through the tulip garden and the old Mughal gardens, watch lotus flowers begin to come up on the lake by summer.

variety: 150 wisteria plants forming tunnels of purple, white, blue
tip: You must buy tickets online in advance during peak season. They sell out.
story: Kawachi Fuji Garden near Kitakyushu is a private garden that has become one of the most photographed places in Japan. Its 150 wisteria plants form tunnels of purple, white, pink, and blue that you walk through — the flowers hanging down all around you at face level, the smell heavy and sweet, bees working through the blooms overhead. You need to buy tickets online in advance during peak season; they sell out weeks ahead. The garden is only open for a few weeks in late April and early May, and again briefly in November for the autumn maples. Go on a weekday morning. The tunnels are narrow, and the garden stays relatively small, so even a moderate crowd feels like a lot. Japanese wisteria — fuji in Japanese — is one of the country's great flowering vines, and the oldest trees at Kawachi are over a hundred years old. The tunnels are the signature, but also walk the larger trellis — a ceiling of color you stand under looking up as if at a stained glass window made of flowers. Stop at the small café for matcha ice cream. Take the train back to Kokura or Hakata — the garden is best as a day trip.

variety: Lavandula angustifolia
tip: Skip Sénanque Abbey — too crowded. Valensole Plateau is equally stunning with a fraction of the tourists.
story: The Valensole Plateau is the lavender heart of Provence — a high, dry plateau north of Aix-en-Provence where the fields roll in straight rows across 800 square kilometers. In late June and July, the whole plateau turns deep purple and the air becomes thick with that unmistakable smell — clean, herbal, a little bittersweet. Skip the Sénanque Abbey photos you see on every Pinterest board; it's beautiful but mobbed. Valensole plateau is just as stunning and gives you whole valleys of lavender without the crowds. Rent a car in Aix, pack a picnic of bread, local cheese, and a bottle of rosé, and drive the small roads between the fields. Stop wherever the light looks best. Small distilleries along the way sell lavender oil, honey made by bees working the fields, sachets of dried lavender. Buy some. The local honey — miel de lavande — is the best souvenir. Lavender season peaks in early July; the fields are harvested mechanically by mid-July, so the purple is gone within weeks. Time your visit. Stay in a farmhouse B&B — a mas — and wake to the smell already in the room, rising off the fields just outside the window.

variety: Poppies, cornflowers, lentil flowers — rainbow meadow
tip: The Piana di Castelluccio sits at 1,450m elevation. Bring layers even in summer.
story: Castelluccio di Norcia sits at 1,450 meters on a plateau in the Sibillini Mountains of Umbria, and for four or five weeks in late June and early July the plain below it turns into what locals call la fiorita — the bloom. Poppies, cornflowers, violets, yellow mustard, wild lentils — a rainbow meadow stretching for thousands of hectares under the Apennines. The village itself is tiny, still rebuilding from the 2016 earthquake, but the plain is permanent. Bring layers even in summer; the elevation keeps it cool. Drive the switchback road up from Norcia at dawn to see the colors in the first light — the plain fills with pink, blue, yellow, red, all mixed, and the poppies especially seem to move with the wind in a way that makes the whole field look alive. The local lentils, grown between the flowers, are some of the most prized in Italy. Buy a bag. Have a long lunch at one of the small trattorias in Norcia — the cured meats here are famous — and come back for the second-best light at sunset. Few places in Europe have this kind of wildness anymore. La fiorita remains one of them.

variety: Helianthus annuus — rolling golden hills
tip: The road between San Quirico d'Orcia and Pienza has the most photogenic fields with cypress trees.
story: The Val d'Orcia is the Tuscany you've seen in every movie — cypress-lined roads, stone farmhouses on hilltops, slow turns of land unfolding toward more hills. Sunflowers are a summer crop here, and in June and July the rolling fields turn gold, wave after wave, against the darker green of the cypresses. The road between San Quirico d'Orcia and Pienza has the most photographed fields, and the road toward Bagno Vignoni runs past smaller patches tucked into valleys. Tuscan farmers grow sunflowers mostly for oil — girasole — and the plants follow the sun through the morning and then face east again at evening. The bloom itself lasts only two or three weeks before the heads droop and the seeds set. Stay in one of the agriturismi — working farms that take guests — and wake early for the best light. Sip an espresso on the terrace. The hills are soft gold in the first sun, deeper gold by mid-morning, and by noon everything washes out in the heat. Eat a long Tuscan lunch of pici and pecorino, nap in the afternoon like a sensible person, and go back out at sunset when everything turns to honey.

variety: Lupine, avalanche lily, paintbrush, glacier lily
tip: Hurricane Ridge is the most accessible meadow. The Obstruction Point road has fewer people.
story: Olympic National Park in Washington holds several small worlds — rainforests on one side, high subalpine meadows on the other. In July and August, the meadows at Hurricane Ridge fill with avalanche lilies, Indian paintbrush, lupine, beargrass, and glacier lilies. From the ridge you look out across the Olympic Mountains on one side, the Strait of Juan de Fuca on the other, and Vancouver Island beyond that. Hurricane Ridge is the most accessible meadow — a paved road goes right to it. For fewer people, drive farther along the gravel Obstruction Point Road; the meadows there are just as spectacular and almost always empty. The wildflowers here are short-lived: snow melts late, and summer is compressed into eight weeks. Check the park's meadow bloom report before you go. Deer and marmots come close; black bears are possible but not a real worry on the main trails. Pack a proper picnic — bread, cheese, a thermos of coffee — and eat it on one of the benches at Hurricane Ridge looking at the glaciers across the valley. The Pacific Northwest does alpine the way few places do. You leave with your lungs clean.

variety: Leontopodium alpinum and Siberian wildflowers
tip: The Great Baikal Trail on the southwestern shore passes through the best wildflower meadows.
story: Lake Baikal holds a fifth of the world's fresh water — a trench of a lake, more than a mile deep in places, so clear that in winter you can see down through the ice for thirty meters. In summer, the southern and western shores come into flower. Edelweiss, the small woolly mountain flower of the Alps, also grows here. So do Siberian gentians, wild irises, scillas, and a dozen other species you'll not see anywhere else. The Great Baikal Trail on the southwestern shore is the best walking — hundreds of kilometers of path through taiga and alpine meadow with the lake a silver sheet below. Base yourself in Listvyanka or take the longer train to Olkhon Island. The Buryat communities around the lake have a deep spiritual relationship with it; the shamanist traditions are still alive. Eat omul, the endemic whitefish, smoked over birch. Drink a glass of herbal Siberian tea. The nights are short this far north in July, and the flowers bloom under low golden light that seems to go on forever. Baikal is older than almost any lake on Earth — 25 million years — and its flowers hold that ancient hush.

variety: Edelweiss, blue poppies, wild roses at 4,000m+
tip: Combine with the Markha Valley trek. You might spot a snow leopard too.
story: Ladakh is a cold desert at 3,500 meters and higher, and yet every July its valleys surprise visitors with wildflowers. Edelweiss, blue poppies, wild roses, gentians, and anemones grow at altitudes where you wouldn't expect anything to grow. Hemis National Park is the largest high-altitude park in India and the stronghold of the snow leopard, though sightings are rare. What you will see: miles of rolling valleys covered in little bright flowers, old Buddhist monasteries clinging to cliffs, yaks grazing in the distance. The Markha Valley trek is a classic eight-day circuit that passes through the best meadows. Combine it with a few days in Leh to acclimatize first — Leh is itself at 3,500m, and altitude is no joke. The monasteries around Leh — Thiksey, Hemis, Alchi — are breathtaking even if you do nothing else. Eat thukpa and momos in small family kitchens. Drink butter tea. Ladakh opens to visitors only from June through September; the rest of the year the passes close with snow. The wildflowers here are tough, small, and fierce — they have the whole winter to survive and only ten weeks to bloom, and they make the most of it.

variety: Gentian, alpine roses, edelweiss, buttercups
tip: Take the Jungfrau Railway to Kleine Scheidegg. The meadows along the hiking trail to Männlichen are extraordinary.
story: Grindelwald sits in a green bowl beneath the north face of the Eiger, and from late June through July the surrounding meadows become a textbook of Alpine botany. Gentians, alpine roses, edelweiss, buttercups, globeflowers, orchids, and a hundred other species fill the slopes, and the cowbells from the traditional dairy herds drift across the valley. Take the Jungfrau Railway up to Kleine Scheidegg. The hike from there to Männlichen runs along a high trail with the Eiger, Mönch, and Jungfrau on one side and flower-filled slopes on the other. The path is easy enough for anyone steady on their feet. Stop for lunch at Männlichen — the ridge has a small restaurant with rösti and bratwurst and cold beer, and a terrace with a view that will not let you look away. The Swiss keep these meadows working — they're grazed and cut in traditional rotations, which is what makes the wildflower diversity possible. Stay in one of the wooden chalets in Grindelwald village. Walk slowly. Take a cold drink to one of the mountain benches in the afternoon. Alpine summer is short and generous, and this particular corner of it is one of the most beautiful places Europe has.

variety: Lupinus nootkatensis — purple and blue
tip: Under the midnight sun, you can photograph lupins at 2am with golden light.
story: The Lofoten Islands sit above the Arctic Circle — a chain of dramatic granite peaks rising straight out of cold sea. In late June and early July, the roadsides, meadows, and old farms fill with Lupinus nootkatensis, blue and purple lupins that stand tall against the dark rock and blue water. And because the sun never quite sets this far north in midsummer, you can photograph the lupins at 2 a.m. in a golden light that simply continues. The midnight sun does something strange to your sense of time — you sleep when you're tired, eat when you're hungry, forget to check your watch. Drive the E10 road that connects the islands. Stop at Reine, Henningsvær, and the fishing villages with their red wooden rorbuer cabins. Eat fresh cod caught that morning. Walk one of the hiking trails through lupin meadows — the Kvalvika Beach hike takes you over a saddle into a hidden cove. Norwegians have a complicated relationship with lupins, technically invasive, but you'll be looking at them and loving them regardless. The combination of Arctic light, granite peaks, turquoise water, and walls of lupin is not something you can photograph well. You have to stand in it.

variety: 600+ species including Brahma Kamal, Blue Poppy
tip: Stay in Ghangaria village. Start the 17km trek at dawn — flowers are most vibrant in early morning light.
story: The Valley of Flowers is a high Himalayan valley in Uttarakhand — a glacier-fed meadow at 3,500 meters where more than 600 species of wildflowers bloom between July and September. Brahma Kamal, the sacred mountain lotus. The blue Himalayan poppy. Marsh marigolds, primulas, Himalayan balsam, a dozen kinds of orchid. It's a UNESCO World Heritage site, and visiting it is one of the great walking experiences in India. The trek starts from Govindghat and climbs 17 kilometers through pine forest to the village of Ghangaria, which is where you sleep. From Ghangaria the final 4 km into the valley begins early the next morning, when the flowers are most vibrant in the soft light. The trail is steady but not technical, and local porters can help with bags. The journey from the plains is part of the gift: a flight to Dehradun, a slow drive up through Rishikesh, three or four days at the monastery town of Govindghat, and then the walk into a valley of flowers waist-high.

variety: Four varieties of lavender + rainbow flower hills
tip: The Irodori field has seven colors of flowers in striped rows with mountains behind. Free entry.
story: Farm Tomita in Furano, Hokkaido is the oldest working lavender farm in Japan — they've been growing it here since 1958, long before it became famous. In July, the farm opens its rainbow fields: stripes of lavender, salvia, poppy, marigold, gypsophila running down the hillside in color bands that look painted. The Irodori field is the signature — seven colors in straight rows with the Tokachi mountains behind. Go early in the day. A small café on the farm serves lavender ice cream and a milky Hokkaido soft-serve that is probably the best ice cream in Japan. The farm charges nothing for entry — it's a working farm that happens to also be one of the most beautiful places you can visit in Hokkaido. Stay in Furano town and rent a car; the nearby area is full of other flower farms, ranches, and blue ponds. The lavender harvest begins in late July, and by early August the fields are mostly cut. Time your visit for mid-July when everything is at peak. Buy a small sachet of dried lavender at the shop. Hokkaido in summer is cool and quiet, and a day at Farm Tomita is as close to a perfect summer day as you can arrange.

variety: Nelumbo nucifera — sacred lotus
tip: Take a shikara boat ride at sunrise. The lotus blooms open with the morning light and the whole lake turns pink.
story: Picture this: Dal Lake in Srinagar at dawn, the mountains rising pink behind, the water as still as a held breath, and across wide patches of the surface, lotus flowers opening with the morning light. The sacred lotus — Nelumbo nucifera — has bloomed on Dal Lake for as long as anyone has recorded. The flowers lift themselves above the leaves on long stems, the petals curling open to show deep pink centers, and by mid-morning a whole area of the lake is covered in blossoms. Take a shikara ride at sunrise — the wooden boats are painted in pinks and greens, paddled by quiet men in woolen caps, and they glide through the lotus gardens as the whole valley wakes. Vendors paddle up with hot kahwa in steel cups, or freshly baked kulcha bread, or bunches of yellow lotus stems eaten as a vegetable across Kashmir. This is one of the oldest continuous landscapes in India — the houseboats, the floating gardens, the Mughal shalimar gardens a few kilometers away. Book a houseboat. Spend three days doing almost nothing but watching the lake change color.

variety: Helianthus annuus — vast commercial fields
tip: The road from Seville to Carmona passes through endless sunflower fields. Stop anywhere along the A-4.
story: Carmona is a small hilltop town in Andalusia, less than an hour from Seville, and from mid-June through mid-July the surrounding plains turn solid gold with sunflowers. Spain grows more sunflowers than almost any country in Europe, and this corner of Andalusia holds some of the largest commercial fields. The A-4 highway between Seville and Carmona passes through endless expanses of them — pull off at any of the rest stops and walk a few steps into a field. The sunflowers here are tall, sometimes higher than your head, and they turn together to follow the sun through the day. Carmona itself is worth the trip even without the flowers — Roman ruins, Moorish walls, whitewashed houses, a parador in a former palace. Eat a long Andalusian lunch of gazpacho and grilled fish. Take a siesta. Come back to the fields at golden hour, when the low sun sets the whole plain on fire. Nights here are hot, long, and full of swallows. If you stay in the old town, open your window after dark — the air smells of jasmine and the faint distant fields of sunflowers still standing out in the dark earth.

variety: Vietnamese lotus — pink and white
tip: Rent a bicycle and ride around West Lake in the early morning when lotus vendors sell fresh blooms.
story: West Lake — Hồ Tây — is the largest lake in Hanoi and a quiet counterpoint to the motorbike rush of the old quarter. In June, July, and August, whole sections of the lake fill with lotus flowers. The Vietnamese lotus is slightly smaller than the Indian one, pink and white, and it is woven into Vietnamese culture — on coins, in tea, in painting. Lotus tea — trà sen — is made by packing green tea leaves inside open lotus blossoms overnight so the tea absorbs the perfume. Rent a bicycle and ride the 17-kilometer loop around West Lake at dawn. Vendors paddle small boats between the flower patches, cutting blossoms to sell. Stop at one of the little cafés along the water for a phin-dripped coffee and a bowl of bún ốc — snail noodle soup, a Hanoi specialty. The flowers close at midday heat and open again in the morning, so come early. Older Hanoians remember when the whole lake was pink in July; urban development has reduced the lotus gardens, but a concerted effort has brought them back. The evening here is also beautiful — the lake reflects neon and trees, and the last lotus of the day closes slowly as the sun goes down.

variety: Columbine, lupine, Indian paintbrush — Wildflower Capital of Colorado
tip: The Judd Falls trail and Rustler Gulch are the best wildflower hikes.
story: Crested Butte calls itself the Wildflower Capital of Colorado, and in July it earns the title. The high meadows above town fill with columbine, lupine, Indian paintbrush, mule's ear, larkspur, fireweed, and a hundred other Rocky Mountain natives. The annual Wildflower Festival in mid-July offers guided walks, flower photography workshops, and talks from local botanists. The Judd Falls trail is short and easy and passes through some of the densest patches; Rustler Gulch is a longer, harder hike that takes you deep into a flower-filled basin with waterfalls. Come in early to mid-July. The bloom varies year to year — snowpack determines when things open — but most summers peak in the first two weeks of July. Crested Butte itself is a Victorian mining town turned ski resort turned summer paradise, with ice cream shops, a good brewpub, and a strong sense of itself. The elk bugle in September but the meadows bloom in July. Stay a few nights. Hike early in the morning before the afternoon thunderstorms roll in off the mountains. Eat a big breakfast afterward — huevos rancheros or a proper American diner plate. The Rockies in summer are one of the great secrets of North American travel.

variety: Blue and purple hydrangeas lining every road
tip: Drive any road on the island — hydrangeas line the hedgerows everywhere. Sete Cidades crater lake has the most dramatic backdrop.
story: São Miguel is the largest of the Azores, an island in the middle of the Atlantic where the hedgerows are not hedgerows but hydrangeas — blue and purple hydrangeas lining every road, cloud to cloud, mile after mile. The plants aren't native; they were introduced centuries ago as ornamentals, and in the volcanic soil and constant mist they took over, replacing stone walls as the most common field boundary. In July and August, the whole island looks like it's been drawn with blue ink. Drive any road — you don't need a plan. The most dramatic stop is Sete Cidades, twin crater lakes ringed by hydrangea-covered hillsides, one blue and one green. Pico do Carvão is another classic viewpoint. Eat cozido das Furnas, a traditional stew cooked in volcanic steam. Swim in the hot springs at Poça da Dona Beija under a canopy of flowers. The Azores are cooler than you'd expect — sweater weather even in summer — and the light is that specific Atlantic light, half silver, half blue. The islands feel like somewhere at the edge of Europe holding its own quiet secrets. The hydrangeas are one of them.

variety: English lavender — rows against honey-colored Cotswold stone villages
tip: Visit Snowshill Lavender Farm then walk to Snowshill village for the quintessential Cotswolds experience.
story: Cotswolds Lavender near Snowshill village grows its lavender in long, orderly rows that crest over a small hill and disappear toward the horizon of honey-colored stone villages. The English do lavender differently from the French — tidier, smaller scale, more gardened — and here the effect is the quintessential Cotswolds postcard. Walk through the fields for the scent and the hum of bees, then take the short stroll into Snowshill itself, one of the prettiest villages in the region — pub, manor house, church with a modest garden. Visit the farm shop for lavender scones, lavender shortbread, lavender lemonade (don't skip it — it's actually good), and the essential oil distilled on-site. Lavender season here runs from late June through the end of July. Go on a weekday if you can. The English countryside in summer is deeply, almost gently beautiful — the kind of landscape that has been cared for continuously for a thousand years. Combine a visit to Cotswolds Lavender with stops at Stow-on-the-Wold, Bourton-on-the-Water, and Chipping Campden. Have afternoon tea somewhere with a view. Bring a light cardigan; English summer evenings cool off quickly. Take a small bottle of the oil home. It smells like a whole valley.

variety: Strobilanthes kunthiana — blooms once every 12 years!
tip: Next bloom expected in 2030. When it happens, the hills turn completely blue-violet. Mark your calendar.
story: This one is magic — a flower that blooms only once every twelve years. The neelakurinji is a small blue-violet shrub that grows on the high hills of the Western Ghats, and when it flowers, the entire Eravikulam National Park above Munnar turns blue-violet. It's so rare that generations of Malayali poets have written about it. The next big bloom is expected in 2030 — worth marking the calendar for. The Muthuvan tribal people who live in these hills traditionally counted their age in neelakurinji blooms. Even outside the mass flowering year, you can visit Eravikulam in August and September to see smaller patches and to look for the nearly-extinct Nilgiri tahr, the small mountain goat that still grazes these slopes. Munnar itself is a tea country town — green tea estates stepping down the valleys, the air thin and cool, small chai shops on every corner. Take a long drive through the estates in the morning when the mist is still rising. Eat a plate of puttu and kadala curry for breakfast. The trip is gentle: a flight to Kochi, a winding drive up into the hills, a few days in a tea plantation guesthouse, waiting for something blue.

variety: 3,500+ species — desert to flower ocean
tip: The flowers follow the sun — face east in morning, west in afternoon. Photograph with sun behind you.
story: Namaqualand is a semi-desert on the western coast of South Africa, bone-dry most of the year, and then for six weeks in August and September it becomes one of the floral wonders of the world. More than 3,500 species bloom at once, dominated by orange Namaqualand daisies but including gazanias, mesembryanthemums, gladioli, and dozens of small succulents. The flowers follow the sun through the day — they face east in the morning and west by afternoon. To photograph them, keep the sun at your back. The bloom depends on winter rainfall. In a good year, the hillsides, plains, and roadside verges become solid orange, yellow, and white. Base yourself in Springbok or in the small town of Kamieskroon, and drive the Skilpad Wildflower Reserve and the Goegap Nature Reserve. The wildflower displays also happen in the West Coast National Park, just north of Cape Town — easier to reach and almost as spectacular. Pack layers; the coastal desert is cold at night. Eat boerewors sausage and drink a glass of pinotage at a small guesthouse. The orange of the daisies against the gray-brown rocks of this ancient landscape is a combination you'll want to keep looking at.

variety: National flower of Mexico — hundreds of varieties
tip: Take a trajinera boat through the canals of Xochimilco to see dahlias in the chinampas (floating gardens).
story: The dahlia is Mexico's national flower, and Xochimilco is the floating-garden neighborhood of Mexico City where dahlias still grow in chinampas — the Aztec-era floating agriculture islands that have been farmed continuously for six hundred years. In autumn, colorful wooden trajinera boats glide through the canals past chinampas blooming with dahlias, marigolds, and lilies. Hire a trajinera — they're brightly painted with girls' names on the prows — and bring snacks and music. A boat with mariachi will likely pull up alongside. Vendors float past with tamales, quesadillas, micheladas, and grilled corn. Xochimilco is officially part of Mexico City but feels like another world — UNESCO heritage, still actively farmed by the families who have been here for generations. The dahlias on the chinampas are cultivated for markets but also for ceremony — the flowers are part of Day of the Dead altars, weddings, weekend picnics. Go on a Saturday in late September or October for the festival atmosphere. Don't rush. A trajinera ride lasts two or three hours — it's designed to be slow. Eat well. Drink a little. Watch the chinampas pass with their walls of flowers. This is old Mexico at its liveliest and most beautiful.

variety: Pink, white, and orange cosmos along riverbanks
tip: The Hangang River bicycle path has long stretches of cosmos on both sides.
story: Cosmos is the autumn flower in Korea. From mid-September through October, riverbanks, parks, and vacant lots across Seoul fill with these tall, delicate pink, white, and orange flowers — simple daisy-shaped blooms on long stems that wave in the breeze. The Hangang River bicycle path is the best introduction — long stretches on both banks with cosmos planted in wide beds, skyscrapers of Seoul rising behind. Olympic Park is another classic spot, with expansive cosmos meadows that feel surprisingly rural given the city just beyond. Rent a city bike and ride the Hangang path on a cool autumn Saturday — the Koreans do autumn well. Stop at one of the convenience stores along the way for a can of coffee and a triangle kimbap, and sit on one of the benches overlooking the river. Cosmos bloom for about six weeks; the peak is the first half of October. Combine with autumn leaf viewing in the nearby Bukhansan mountains. Seoul in October is one of the best cities in the world to walk and eat and look up at mountains — and the cosmos, small, humble, a reminder of the fields outside the city, keep the season honest.

variety: High-altitude wildflowers at 4,718m elevation
tip: Acclimatize in Lhasa first. The altitude at Namtso is serious.
story: Namtso Lake sits at 4,718 meters on the Tibetan Plateau — the world's highest saltwater lake, sacred to Tibetan Buddhists. In August, the meadows around its shores fill with wildflowers — asters in blue and purple, gentians, edelweiss, tiny alpine primulas, and carpets of small red-stemmed flowers. Yaks graze in the distance. Prayer flags strung from rocks flutter in the thin wind. The lake itself is an almost supernatural shade of turquoise, the color of a gem, surrounded by snow-capped peaks. Acclimatize in Lhasa first. Namtso is only reachable by road from Lhasa — a four-hour drive over a 5,190-meter pass — and the altitude is no small matter. Spend two days in Lhasa, drink hot butter tea, visit Jokhang Temple, take the altitude seriously. Then go. Stay overnight at one of the small tent camps on the southern shore; the night sky at this altitude is one of the most star-filled you will ever see. In the morning, walk the kora — the pilgrimage circuit — around Tashi Dor peninsula, the flowers at your feet, the sacred lake below, and the whole roof of the world stretching out in every direction.

variety: Calluna vulgaris — purple moorland
tip: Glen Coe and Rannoch Moor are the most dramatic heather landscapes. Go after a rain for the most intense purple.
story: In August and September, the Scottish Highlands turn purple. Heather — Calluna vulgaris — covers millions of acres of moorland, and the blooming is one of the defining sights of the country. Glen Coe and Rannoch Moor are the most dramatic — wide, open landscapes with mountains rising abruptly out of purple moor. Go after rain for the deepest color; the heather glows. The West Highland Line railway passes through these landscapes, and the four-hour train from Glasgow to Mallaig is one of the most beautiful train journeys anywhere, with heather-covered moors, lochs, and sea-lochs filling every window. Stop for lunch at a pub along the way — Scottish pub food is hearty and often surprisingly good — and try a dram of a peaty single malt. The honey made from heather — fragrant, almost treacly — is the best souvenir. Bring waterproof clothes even in August; Scotland makes its own weather. Walk a section of the West Highland Way if you have the time. The heather underfoot smells faintly herbal when you crush it, and the purple slopes stretch as far as the eye can see. The Highlands in full bloom are a kind of austere, wild beauty that stays with you for years.

variety: 200+ species bloom in the world's driest desert (only in rare rainy years)
tip: This happens only 2-3 times per decade after unusual rainfall. Follow Chilean news to time your visit.
story: The Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on Earth — some weather stations have never recorded rain. And yet, in certain rare years when an unusual storm system pushes south, the seeds that have been waiting for decades wake, and the desert between Copiapó and Vallenar erupts in millions of flowers. The desierto florido — flowering desert — is one of the natural wonders of South America, and it happens only two or three times a decade. Over 200 species can bloom at once: white nolanas, pink pata de guanaco, yellow cebollines, and the deep purple añañuca lily that is the event's unofficial symbol. Follow Chilean news. When a bloom is declared, domestic tourism spikes and hotels fill fast. Fly to Copiapó and drive the small roads. The Llanos de Challe National Park is the official reserve, but the flowers spill out across hundreds of square kilometers. Go early in the morning; the flowers close in the afternoon heat. Bring water — the desert is still a desert. The ocean is just west, and you can end a day of flower-watching by standing on the cliffs above the Pacific as the sun sets. Few landscapes are as improbable as this one.

variety: King Protea, pincushions, ericas — ancient floral kingdom
tip: Walk the Boomslang treetop walkway at Kirstenbosch for aerial views of the fynbos against Table Mountain.
story: Kirstenbosch is one of the great botanical gardens of the world, founded in 1913 on the eastern slopes of Table Mountain, and it holds some of the richest plant diversity on Earth. The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of the six floral kingdoms in the world but one of the most biodiverse — 9,000 plant species, two-thirds of them found nowhere else. Fynbos is the local name for the shrubland that covers the cape, and its star species are the proteas — prehistoric-looking flowers with big woody heads and delicate pointed petals, the King Protea being South Africa's national flower. Walk the Boomslang, the canopy walkway that lifts you above the fynbos with Table Mountain rising behind. Walk the Skeleton Gorge trail for the best wildflower variety — it climbs through old trees, past waterfalls, and up onto the mountain proper. Time your visit for September through November when the spring bloom is at peak. Pack a picnic — the garden lawns were made for this. Eat a proper Cape Malay curry in town afterward. End your day at sunset on the cable car up Table Mountain. Cape Town in spring is something South Africans quietly believe — and they're right — is the best place on Earth.

variety: Frangipani, lotus, heliconia, bougainvillea
tip: The lotus pond at Saraswati Temple in central Ubud is the most photogenic. Visit at opening to avoid crowds.
story: Ubud is the cultural heart of Bali, and flowers are everywhere here — not in fields or gardens so much as woven into daily life. Women make canang sari — small palm-leaf offering baskets of flowers, petals, incense — and place them on the ground outside every shop, temple, and doorway several times a day. Frangipani trees drop their creamy white blossoms onto the paths of the Saraswati Temple, where a huge ornamental lotus pond reflects an old Balinese pavilion. Go to Saraswati at opening, before the tour buses arrive. The lotus opens in the morning with extraordinary dignity, petal by slow petal. Walk the Campuhan Ridge trail for a view over the valley of rice terraces, themselves often bordered by marigolds and heliconias. The rice terraces at Tegalalang, a few kilometers north, are their own kind of flower — geometric, green, and living. Eat a proper rijsttafel at a warung. Drink a fresh young coconut. Bali has a particular kind of slowness, ritual-based, attentive, flower-laced. Even the simplest shopping trip involves offerings — and you begin, after a day or two, to move with the same pace. The lotus, the frangipani, the marigold, the hibiscus — the island holds them all in daily devotion.

variety: 5 million Lycoris radiata — fields of blood-red
tip: Blooms for only 10-14 days each year around the autumn equinox. Check the official website for real-time bloom status.
story: Red spider lilies — higanbana — bloom in Japan for only ten to fourteen days each year, around the autumn equinox. The stems push up bare from the ground, leafless, and the flowers open at the top in fierce scarlet sprays with long, curling stamens. Kinchakuda in Saitama Prefecture holds five million higanbana in a meandering grove by a river, and during the two weeks of bloom the forest floor becomes a carpet of intense red that glows in the low autumn light. The flower's name literally means 'equinox flower,' and in Japan it is associated with the ancestors — higan is also the Buddhist word for the other shore, the afterlife. You'll see these lilies planted in temple grounds and along rice-field dikes all over Japan. Kinchakuda, though, is the mass display. Check the official website for real-time bloom status before you go — the flowers are so short-lived that a week can change everything. Trains from Tokyo take about ninety minutes. Go on a weekday morning. Walk slowly through the grove. The red is the red you remember from certain dreams, and the light filtering through the trees above turns every flower into a small lit torch.

variety: 600+ dahlia plants in Golden Gate Park
tip: The dahlia garden is behind the Conservatory — most visitors miss it entirely.
story: San Francisco's Conservatory of Flowers is the oldest Victorian glass greenhouse in North America, a white wedding cake of a building that has been tended in Golden Gate Park since 1879. Most tourists visit the conservatory itself for the orchids and tropicals. Almost no one notices that just behind it is the Golden Gate Park Dahlia Garden — 600+ dahlia plants in an open-air display that's one of the best urban dahlia gardens in the United States. The dahlia is San Francisco's official flower, and the garden volunteers tend it through the summer, with the blooms peaking from September through mid-October. The varieties are staggering — dinner-plate dahlias the size of a face, pom-poms, cactus-formed, bicolored. Walk through in the early morning; the fog often hangs heavy in the park until mid-day. Bring coffee. The Japanese Tea Garden next door opens at the same time and is even more beautiful in the fog.
