San Francisco's microclimate means the dahlias bloom later and longer than almost anywhere else — a small perk of its famously cold summers. Don't miss the dahlia garden. It is one of those quiet civic pleasures that feels handmade, tended by volunteers because they love it.

variety: Jacaranda mimosifolia — purple canopy over entire town
tip: See Jacaranda Avenue and the Grafton Bridge. The annual festival includes a Jacaranda Queen crowning.
story: Grafton in northern New South Wales is known in Australia as the Jacaranda City — an entire town taken over by a single flowering tree species. In late October and November, 5,000 jacaranda trees bloom simultaneously, carpeting the streets in purple petals and forming a continuous canopy overhead. The town holds the country's oldest floral festival, now over ninety years running, complete with the crowning of a Jacaranda Queen. Walk Jacaranda Avenue, drive across the Grafton Bridge with purple on both sides, sit in the parks where the trees drop petals onto the grass until the whole ground looks like a violet lake. The Clarence River runs through the city and reflects the blossoms. Jacarandas are not native to Australia — they were introduced from Argentina in the nineteenth century — but they've found the Australian climate and soil so agreeable that cities up and down the east coast have adopted them. Grafton's festival is the most celebratory version. Come for the first weekend of November for the full program. Eat a sausage sandwich at the fair, watch the parade, walk under the purple ceilings in the evening when the streetlights come on. It's a small-town festival of a flower that has become a local love.

variety: Imperial chrysanthemum exhibition — Japan's national flower
tip: The autumn chrysanthemum exhibition has been running since 1878. Combine with autumn leaf viewing.
story: The chrysanthemum is the imperial flower of Japan — the sixteen-petaled gold chrysanthemum is the emblem of the Imperial Household — and the annual autumn chrysanthemum exhibition at Shinjuku Gyoen has been staged continuously since 1878. The show is unlike anything you've seen. Traditional Japanese chrysanthemum training produces specimens that look almost architectural — single plants with hundreds of perfect blooms arranged in cascades, cones, and spheres; bonsai-sized miniatures; the famous ōzukuri form where a single plant is trained to show over 500 flowers on one perfect dome. The exhibition runs through November. Go on a weekday morning. Shinjuku Gyoen is one of Tokyo's great parks — 144 acres of French, English, and Japanese garden styles — and in November it's also one of the best places in the city for autumn leaves. Combine the chrysanthemum exhibition with a walk through the maples and ginkgos. Stop at a small tea pavilion for matcha and a wagashi sweet shaped like a chrysanthemum. The discipline involved in training these plants is nearly monastic — years of patient pruning, training, and attention for a display that lasts a few weeks. You come away from Shinjuku Gyoen with a slightly changed sense of what a flower can be.

variety: Tagetes — orange and yellow, used for Diwali garlands
tip: Go at 5am when vendors are arranging fresh flowers. The market is a feast for the eyes and nose.
story: The Dadar flower market is the best in Mumbai, and every October it transforms. From Navratri through Diwali, the market is a river of orange and yellow, mountains of marigolds heaped into brass scales, garlands being threaded by women sitting cross-legged on the pavement, the smell of fresh flowers cutting through the morning city. Go at 5 am. The vendors have been there since 3, arranging their fresh deliveries from Pune and Nashik, and by sunrise the whole market is a photograph. Buy a kilo. Bring it home and string your own garlands. The marigold is the flower of auspicious beginnings across India — a doorway flower, a wedding flower, a festival flower — and during Diwali every threshold in the country wears one. Cross the bridge to Ranade Road for the adjacent flower stalls. Get chai from the little stand at the corner. Walk back through the morning rush. The market hasn't changed much in decades — for many Mumbaikars it's a childhood memory still happening, the same brass scales, the same orange piles, the same morning light.

variety: 5.5 million cosmos flowers across rolling meadows
tip: The park is huge — rent a bicycle at the entrance. The cosmos hill near the Japanese Garden is the best spot.
story: Showa Kinen Park is one of Tokyo's largest parks, 163 hectares in Tachikawa on the western edge of the metropolitan area, and every October it fills with 5.5 million cosmos flowers. The Hara-ga-oka hillside — cosmos hill — is the signature feature, a whole slope of pink, white, and orange cosmos that turns into a pastel quilt in the autumn sun. The park is huge. Rent a bicycle at the entrance and ride between the various gardens — there are also dahlia beds, late roses, and a dedicated Japanese garden that turns gold and red with autumn leaves in November. Bring a picnic. Japanese park food stalls are exceptional, with hot yakisoba, soft serve, and the essential onigiri. The cosmos bloom from late September through early November, with peak around the third week of October. Families come out for hanami-style picnics, couples pose for photos, old men take out easels and paint. The train from central Tokyo takes about forty minutes. Go on a weekday — weekends get very busy — and give yourself a full afternoon. The cosmos are short, delicate, simple flowers, but in the millions they become something else: a pink and white sea, rolling slowly in the wind like an ocean.

variety: 3,000+ species of Western Australian wildflowers
tip: The Kings Park Festival in September is free. The bushland trail has 324 native species in one walk.
story: Kings Park in Perth is one of the largest inner-city parks in the world — 4 square kilometers overlooking the Swan River — and two-thirds of it is left as natural bushland. Three thousand species of Western Australian wildflowers grow inside its borders. Every September, the park hosts a free Wildflower Festival, with guided walks, talks, and enormous displays of the state's floral diversity. Kangaroo paw — Anigozanthos — is Western Australia's floral emblem: tall stems with furry, curved flowers in red, yellow, green, and orange that do look surprisingly like the paw of a small animal. The bushland trails inside the park take you past 324 native species in a single walk. Combine with the nearby Botanic Garden for the cultivated displays. Have a picnic on the lawn with views across the river to Perth's skyline. In September, Perth itself is at its best — warm days, cool nights, blue skies, and wildflowers in every park, roadside, and empty lot. West Australia holds roughly 12,000 wildflower species, more than anywhere in Europe, and the easy sophistication of Kings Park is the perfect introduction. Go in the morning for the coolest walking. The café at the top of Kings Park makes very good flat whites and overlooks the whole city.

variety: 20,000+ jacaranda trees — purple canopy over entire city
tip: Plaza San Martín and Avenida Santa Fe are the most photogenic streets. The purple petals carpet the sidewalks.
story: In November, Buenos Aires turns purple. The city has over 20,000 jacaranda trees, planted throughout the 20th century, and when they bloom simultaneously they form a canopy above boulevards, plazas, and sidewalks that is one of the great urban floral displays. Plaza San Martín is a classic spot, with the old British clock tower rising behind the trees, and Avenida Santa Fe between Recoleta and Palermo is the most photographed stretch. The trees shed their leaves before flowering, so the purple is unbroken — the whole canopy floats unattached to any green. Purple petals carpet the sidewalks, cling to car windshields, collect in the gutters. It's messy, and Buenos Aires loves every bit of it. November weather is warm and dry, perfect for walking. Eat long lunches. Do the late dinners. Go to a milonga and watch Argentines tango until 2 am. Stop at the old Paris-style cafés — Café Tortoni, La Biela, Las Violetas — for coffee under ceiling fans. Walk the Rose Garden in Palermo, which is at its peak the same time as the jacarandas. Buenos Aires is one of the great walking cities, and the jacaranda season turns every walk into something memorable.

variety: Russell lupins — purple, pink, yellow against turquoise glacial lake
tip: The Church of the Good Shepherd with lupins in the foreground and lake behind is the iconic shot. Go at sunrise.
story: Lake Tekapo sits in the middle of New Zealand's South Island — a glacial lake so turquoise it looks unreal, ringed by brown-gold tussock hills and snow-capped peaks. In late November and December, Russell lupins cover the lake's shores in spires of purple, pink, yellow, and blue. The Church of the Good Shepherd, a tiny stone chapel built in 1935, stands right at the water's edge. A photograph of the church with lupins in the foreground and the turquoise lake behind is one of New Zealand's iconic images. Go at sunrise. Lupins are technically an invasive species here — they've spread aggressively since being introduced — so don't let any New Zealander hear you celebrate them too loudly. Stay overnight in Tekapo village. The night skies above the lake are a designated International Dark Sky Reserve, and the Milky Way runs straight over the summits of the Southern Alps like a ribbon. The Mount John Observatory has guided astronomy tours. Eat breakfast at the café on the hill, with lupins out one window and the lake out the other. Drive south to Mount Cook the next day; the road passes lupin-edged lakes and rivers the whole way. New Zealand knows how to surprise you.

variety: 70,000+ jacaranda trees lining city streets
tip: Herbert Baker Street in Groenkloof has the most dramatic tunnel of purple. Locals call it Jacaranda City.
story: Pretoria is known across South Africa as the Jacaranda City — 70,000 jacaranda trees line its streets, and when they bloom in October and November, the whole city turns purple. There is a local legend, told to every university student in Pretoria: if a jacaranda flower falls on your head during exam season, you'll pass. The trees were planted in the early 1900s and are now so integral to the city that Pretoria's streets are navigated partly by their colors. Herbert Baker Street in Groenkloof has the most dramatic tunnel of purple, where the canopies meet over the street and form a cathedral of flowers. Union Buildings, the seat of government, has jacarandas on its lawns with views over the city. The bloom peaks in late October. Pretoria weather in October is warm, dry, and clear. Eat a long lunch at Café Riche, one of the oldest cafés in the country. Walk through Church Square. Drive the residential streets for the density of flowers. The city's energy during jacaranda season is genuinely celebratory — weddings, engagement photos, families out walking under the purple ceilings. Pretoria and Johannesburg are only an hour apart, making this an easy add-on to any South African trip.

variety: Muhlenbergia capillaris — pink clouds of ornamental grass
tip: Climb the 291 steps to the Sky Park observation deck for aerial views of the pink muhly fields.
story: Pink muhly grass — Muhlenbergia capillaris — is not a flower technically but an ornamental grass that seeds in clouds of soft pink. Haneul Park (Sky Park) sits on top of what used to be Seoul's largest landfill, now reclaimed and landscaped into one of the city's most unusual green spaces. In October and early November, the pink muhly fields at the top of the park turn into candy-colored pink clouds that move in the wind like something dreamed. Climb the 291 steps to the observation deck for aerial views of the pink fields with downtown Seoul and the Han River beyond. Go at sunset. The low golden light catches the grass from behind and turns the whole field into soft fire. The park is part of the larger World Cup Park complex — the 2002 FIFA World Cup was hosted here. Combine with a visit to the old Hanok village nearby. Koreans call this grass color bunhongsaek — pink — and the social media boom around pink muhly has brought it from a Korean obscurity to a national autumn destination. Dress warmly in late October; Seoul's autumn evenings get crisp. The sky above the park, over the pink grass, is usually that deep Korean autumn blue that feels almost polished.

variety: 300+ varieties across 600 acres
tip: Combine with a visit to the ancient water town of Wuzhen, 15 minutes away.
story: Tongxiang in Zhejiang Province holds one of China's oldest and largest chrysanthemum festivals — 300 varieties across 600 acres, with cultivation going back to the Tang Dynasty. Chrysanthemums in China have a completely different status than in the West: they're one of the Four Gentlemen of classical Chinese painting (along with plum, orchid, and bamboo), a symbol of integrity and scholarly virtue. Tongxiang grows both ornamental and medicinal varieties, and in November the town smells of fresh hangbaiju — the white chrysanthemums dried for tea. Buy a small box. The tea is mild, faintly floral, and considered cooling in traditional Chinese medicine. The festival runs from late October through late November and includes cut-flower exhibitions, poetry readings under the blooms, and nighttime illumination displays. Combine a visit with a day in Wuzhen, the ancient water town just fifteen minutes away — stone bridges, wooden lanterns, canals reflecting old courtyard houses. The combination of Wuzhen's timeless streets and Tongxiang's chrysanthemum exhibition makes for one of the most atmospheric autumn trips in China. Take a slow dinner of freshwater crab and river fish. Walk the old town after dark. The chrysanthemum is a quiet flower, a scholar's flower, and its celebration here is just as quietly beautiful.

variety: Metrosideros excelsa — crimson flowers
tip: Cathedral Cove has ancient pōhutukawa clinging to sea cliffs with red flowers against turquoise water.
story: Pōhutukawa is the New Zealand Christmas tree — Metrosideros excelsa — a gnarled coastal tree that erupts in crimson flowers every December, just in time for summer Christmas in the southern hemisphere. The trees cling to rocky coasts and sea cliffs, and in full bloom they look like torches against the dark green foliage and turquoise water. The Coromandel Peninsula, a two-hour drive from Auckland, has some of the most spectacular pōhutukawa. Cathedral Cove in particular has ancient trees leaning out over the sea, their red flowers brushing the waves below. Walk the coastal track to the cove early in the morning — the path is closed sometimes in the late afternoon for the seabirds. Swim in the cove with the pōhutukawa blazing above you. For Māori, the pōhutukawa has deep significance; at Cape Reinga, a single ancient pōhutukawa is said to be where departing souls slide down into the sea on their journey to the ancestral homeland. Travel slowly around the Coromandel. Stop at Hot Water Beach, where at low tide you can dig your own hot spring in the sand. Eat a paua fritter. Watch the red flowers fall into the green sea, slowly, as summer properly begins.

variety: Euphorbia pulcherrima — native to Mexico, growing wild up to 4m tall
tip: In Taxco, poinsettias grow as large trees along hillside roads, not in pots. The annual Poinsettia Fair is in December.
story: The poinsettia is Mexican, and in Taxco — the silver town carved into the Guerrero hillsides — it grows wild as a tree. Not a potted plant. Not a holiday decoration. A three-meter tree with scarlet bracts blazing in December sun. The Aztecs called it cuetlaxochitl and used its milky sap as medicine. Joel Roberts Poinsett, the first US ambassador to Mexico, brought the plant north in 1828 and attached his name to it. But here, in the towns of southern Mexico, it has always been cuetlaxochitl — a wild and generous thing. Taxco holds an annual Nochebuena festival in early December, and the whole city dresses in its cobbled, silversmith charm. Walk up to the top of the Santa Prisca church viewpoint. Drive the mountain roads where the wild poinsettias bloom along the shoulders. Eat cecina norteña and drink Mexican hot chocolate at one of the small town cafés. Taxco is one of those pueblos mágicos that Mexico does so well — white buildings, red-tiled roofs, narrow stone streets, and silver jewelry workshops in every other doorway. The poinsettias bloom from mid-November through February. You'll go home with a small ceramic figure of a saint, a pair of silver earrings, and a completely changed understanding of a flower you thought you knew.

variety: Prunus cerasoides — winter-blooming cherry
tip: Yuantong Temple and the campus of Yunnan University have the best winter cherry blossom displays.
story: Kunming is Yunnan's capital, nicknamed the Spring City for its mild, year-round climate, and its winter cherry blossoms are one of the small miracles of China. While the rest of the country is in overcoats and scarves, Kunming's winter cherry — Prunus cerasoides — comes into pale pink bloom in December and January. The Yuantong Temple grounds hold some of the oldest winter cherries, and the campus of Yunnan University has a famous avenue of cherries that becomes a pink tunnel. It's not the scale of Jinhae or Washington, but it has its own quiet loveliness — trees blooming in winter light, old men playing mahjong on stone tables underneath, students walking to class. Kunming in January is sunny, dry, and around 15-20°C during the day. Eat a bowl of guoqiao mixian — crossing-the-bridge noodles, a Yunnan classic — for lunch. Walk the Green Lake park, where migratory seagulls from Siberia winter each year in huge flocks, unafraid of people. Combine with Dali and Lijiang for a longer Yunnan trip, or just spend three days in Kunming itself. The winter cherries aren't world-famous, and that's part of their charm. You find them yourself, in a garden behind a temple, and they feel private.

variety: King Protea (national flower) + summer fynbos
tip: Hike Skeleton Gorge for the best wildflower variety. The cable car route has King Protea near the upper station.
story: Cape Town's summer — December through February, southern hemisphere style — is when the mountain behind the city is at its wildest. The King Protea, South Africa's national flower, blooms in the fynbos at higher elevations. The Skeleton Gorge trail is the best wildflower hike up Table Mountain — it begins in the Kirstenbosch gardens and climbs through a wooded ravine, crossing streams, ending at the top plateau where the fynbos spreads out in every direction. The wildflowers in summer are more scattered than in the spring Namaqualand bloom, but the proteas, pincushions, and ericas you do find are spectacular. The upper cable car station is another good spot — King Protea grows right near the top, huge-headed and prehistoric. Take the cable car up and walk a portion of the summit trails. The views over Cape Town, the Atlantic, and the distant mountains of the Cape Peninsula are some of the best in the world. Pack water and sunscreen; summer sun at the top of Table Mountain is serious. Eat at the Table Mountain Café for a view over the city. The fynbos kingdom is one of the rarest floral biomes on Earth, and standing in it with the Atlantic Ocean below is a very specific kind of lucky.

variety: Magenta, orange, white, purple cascading over walls and arches
tip: The old city walls near Nahargarh Fort are draped in bougainvillea. Best photographed in late afternoon golden light.
story: Jaipur in the dry winter months is wrapped in bougainvillea. The pink, magenta, orange, and white papery flowers cascade over the walls of the old city, over the arches of the Hawa Mahal, over the windowsills of haveli guesthouses, over the stone bases of Nahargarh Fort looking down on everything. The Rajput architects of three centuries ago didn't design with bougainvillea in mind — the plant was introduced later — but it has adopted their rose-pink walls and fluted pavilions as if it were always meant to be here. Walk the old city at late afternoon, in the golden hour, when the light catches the flowers and the pink walls and everything glows. Stop at the Amber Fort overlook for the classic view. Eat a thali at LMB in Johari Bazaar. Buy a jar of pickle, a length of block-printed cotton. The rooftop cafés behind the City Palace serve chai and curries with the whole pink city spread below. Bougainvillea needs heat, sun, and very little water — perfect for the dry Rajasthan winter — and it blooms almost continuously from October through March. An easy weekend: a morning train from Delhi, three days in Jaipur, a slow breakfast every morning on a haveli rooftop, and bougainvillea everywhere.

variety: Epiphyllum oxypetalum — night-blooming, wilts by dawn
tip: Ask locally — the flower cannot be sold and only someone with a plant can tell you when it's about to bloom. Visit around 10pm.
story: The Kadupul is not a flower you chase — it chooses you. The night-blooming Epiphyllum oxypetalum grows in the humid air of Kandy and the hill country of Sri Lanka, and it blooms for only a few hours, always at night, always rarely. By dawn the flower has wilted and fallen. Buddhist tradition tells of celestial beings descending to earth to offer the Kadupul to the Buddha, and the flower is so treasured that locally it has no market price — it cannot be sold because it cannot be given meaningfully. To see one, you have to know someone with a plant. Kandy's small hill gardens are where they often grow — tucked into courtyards, coaxed along vine frames, watched all summer by patient owners. Ask at your guesthouse. Ask at a Buddhist temple. Someone will know of a plant expected to bloom this month. Go late at night, around 10 or 11 pm. The flower opens slowly, a large, trumpet-shaped bloom of pure white, with a fragrance that's sweet and heady and doesn't match any other flower. By morning it is a soft white rag on the ground. It's the most ephemeral beauty you'll ever see in your life.

location: Garden of the Sleeping Giant, Nadi
variety: Hibiscus rosa-sinensis — Fiji's national flower
tip: Visit the Garden of the Sleeping Giant in the hills above Nadi — 2,000+ orchids and hibiscus, a garden started by Raymond Burr in the 1970s.
story: The hibiscus is Fiji's national flower, and though it blooms all year round in the islands' gentle climate, the Fiji Hibiscus Festival in Nadi each August celebrates it with proper flair. The gardens in and around Nadi — at the Garden of the Sleeping Giant, at the coastal resorts, at family-run nurseries — overflow with hibiscus in colors that range from pale yellow to deep crimson to soft pink to an almost luminous orange. The Fijian name for the flower is senitoa, and women still tuck it behind an ear on their walk to the market — behind the right ear for single, behind the left for partnered. Visit the Garden of the Sleeping Giant on the slopes above Nadi — Raymond Burr, the actor who played Perry Mason, built this orchid and hibiscus garden in the 1970s, and it has been maintained ever since. A short trail winds through orchids, ferns, and hibiscus spilling over wooden bridges. The Fiji dry season — roughly May through October — is the most comfortable time to visit. Eat fresh coconut at a roadside stand. Drink a bowl of kava. Say bula to everyone you meet. The hibiscus is a flower of everyday beauty here, and Fiji's relationship with it is affectionate and unfussy.

location: Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden, Chiang Mai
variety: Dendrobium, Vanda, Cattleya, Phalaenopsis — over 1,000 species
tip: Take the canopy walkway at the Queen Sirikit garden for epiphytic orchids at treetop height.
story: Chiang Mai is the orchid capital of Thailand. In the cool northern winter — December through February — the gardens around the old city burst into orchid bloom. The Queen Sirikit Botanic Garden in Mae Rim, twenty minutes north of Chiang Mai, has the most comprehensive collection — glasshouses full of Dendrobium, Vanda, Cattleya, Phalaenopsis, and the rare lady's slipper orchids of the northern Thai forests. The garden's canopy walkway takes you through the forest at treetop height, past epiphytic orchids clinging to branches the way they grow in the wild. Small commercial orchid farms line the road north of Chiang Mai. You can buy a plant to ship home, or just walk through rows of 10,000 blooms at once. Thai people have a particular devotion to orchids — the flower appears in garlands, spa treatments, ceremonial offerings, and on most restaurant plates as a garnish. Combine orchid gardens with a morning at Doi Suthep temple and an afternoon cooking class in the old city. Eat a bowl of khao soi. Visit the Sunday walking market. The cool season in Chiang Mai is the best travel time of the year in northern Thailand — dry, breezy, and softly perfumed by flowers every morning when the gardens wake up.

variety: Delonix regia — scarlet canopies over streets
tip: The Esplanade along Darwin Harbour and the residential streets of Parap and Fannie Bay have the densest flame tree cover.
story: Darwin in the Top End of Australia runs on its own seasons: the dry from May to October, and the wet from November to April. Between them — October through December — the flame trees come into full bloom. Delonix regia is also called the royal poinciana or the gulmohar, and when it flowers, the tropical city turns scarlet. Whole streets and parks erupt in the deep orange-red canopies. The Darwin Botanic Gardens has some of the oldest flame trees in the city; the Esplanade looking out over Darwin Harbour is lined with them; the residential streets of Parap and Fannie Bay run under continuous fire-red ceilings. Flame tree flowers are bigger than you expect — delicate, orchid-like, with white-splashed upper petals — and they fall in constant gentle drifts so the ground beneath each tree is also scarlet. Darwin is the closest Australian city to Asia, and the flame tree, native to Madagascar but loved across tropical Asia and Africa, fits here perfectly. Eat at the Mindil Beach sunset markets. Drink a cold beer at one of the waterfront bars. Take a day trip to Litchfield National Park for waterfalls. And when you're walking the city, look up often — the fire overhead is one of the great things about Darwin in spring.

variety: Strelitzia reginae — Madeira's unofficial symbol
tip: Take the cable car from Funchal's old town up to Monte for one of the most beautiful rides in the world, then walk the tropical garden.
story: Madeira is sometimes called the floating garden of the Atlantic, and Funchal, its capital, is full of flowers year-round. The bird of paradise — Strelitzia reginae — grows so abundantly on the island that it has become an informal symbol of Madeira. The flower is unmistakable: orange sepals and blue petals arranged to look like the head of a tropical bird, held up on a long green stem that looks like a plant's idea of a beak. The Monte Palace Madeira Tropical Garden, high above Funchal, has some of the best displays. Take the cable car up from the old town — the ride is one of the world's most beautiful — and spend an afternoon walking through terraced gardens of birds of paradise, orchids, camellias, and proteas, with views across Funchal's red tile roofs to the Atlantic. The Madeira winter — December to March — is the peak bloom season. It's also when you'll still see the terraced hillsides below Funchal green with vegetables and flowers tended by small farmers. Eat espetada, beef skewers grilled on bay laurel branches. Drink a glass of Madeira wine. Ride the wicker toboggans down from Monte, a tradition that started in the 1800s. The island is small, kind, and constantly in flower.

variety: Hoa Đào — pink peach, essential for Tết celebrations
tip: Ride the Ha Giang Loop on a motorbike over three or four days for the full spring experience through Hmong and Dao villages.
story: Ha Giang is the northernmost province of Vietnam, a region of steep karst peaks and terraced rice fields and mountain roads that switch back on themselves for miles. In February and March, around the Tết Lunar New Year, the peach trees of the region flower in soft pink — đào — and the highland villages of the Hmong, Dao, and Tay peoples celebrate with markets, music, and flower branches carried home to every house. A peach blossom branch in the house during Tết is tradition; it brings luck for the year. Ride the Ha Giang Loop — a three or four-day motorbike circuit that takes you through the highest mountain passes in Vietnam — and you'll pass village after village with peach trees bright pink against the gray limestone cliffs. Dong Van, Meo Vac, and Lung Cu Flag Tower are the classic stops. Eat thang co, the Hmong stew, at a market. Drink the local rice wine poured from plastic bottles. Sleep in a stilt-house homestay. The peach blossom season in Ha Giang coincides with the canola and pear blooms of the same highlands, and the whole region becomes a rainbow for a few short weeks. Travel slowly. This is one of the most beautiful corners of Southeast Asia.

variety: Nelumbo nucifera — sacred pink and white lotus
tip: Take the first boat of the day across Lake Pichola before the morning light softens. The view of the City Palace from the water at dawn is the image you'll keep.
story: Udaipur is a city of seven lakes, and in the rainy and post-monsoon months, all of them come into lotus. Lake Pichola, Fateh Sagar, Swaroop Sagar — the blooms spread across quiet bays, the flowers pink and white and sacred. The Mewar royal families built their palaces around these waters, and today you can ride a boat across Pichola past the Jag Mandir and Jagniwas palaces, lotus-edged shores on either side. Go at dawn. The mist is still on the water, the city's white palaces turn pink in the first light, and the lotus flowers open slowly as the day arrives. The Sahelion ki Bari — the Garden of the Maidens — has a small lotus pool with marble cenotaphs at its center; the City Palace has gardens overlooking Pichola's lotus-strewn water. Have a cup of chai at the rooftop of a haveli, looking down. Udaipur's Rajput culture has honored the lotus in architecture, painting, and poetry for centuries. You'll recognize the motif on a hundred surfaces once you've seen it on the lake itself. A train from Delhi, three days of slow boats and palace hotels, marigold sellers and evening kathak performances, and lotus opening every morning on the water.

variety: Yulan, Saucer, and 100+ other magnolia varieties — 10,000 trees
tip: The Moshan Scenic Area on the south shore of East Lake has the densest magnolia plantings. Go on a weekday morning.
story: East Lake — Donghu — is one of China's largest urban lakes, curving through the city of Wuhan and ringed by hills, gardens, and walking paths. In March and April, the magnolia trees around the lake come into bloom — cup-shaped blossoms of pure white, pink, purple, and the deep Yulan magnolia, a variety cultivated in China for over a thousand years. The magnolia gardens at East Lake contain over 10,000 trees and 100 varieties, making it one of the largest magnolia collections in the world. The Yulan — Magnolia denudata — is particularly tied to Chinese classical culture; the blossoms are often depicted in paintings and painted onto porcelain. Walk the lake's Moshan Scenic Area for the highest concentration of flowering trees. The best time is usually mid-March, before the cherries begin and while the magnolias hold their peak. Combine with a visit to the Yellow Crane Tower, Wuhan's most famous landmark, and a bowl of reganmian — hot dry noodles, Wuhan's signature breakfast dish. The Tang-era poet Cui Hao wrote a famous poem at the Yellow Crane Tower, and you can still feel the quiet literary sense of the city, especially in the spring when magnolia petals are drifting down onto old pavilions and slow river water.

variety: 350,000 plum trees, including the prized green-calyx Lü'e variety
tip: Combine with the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum on the same hillside. The plum fragrance is strongest in the early morning.
story: Plum Blossom Hill — Meihua Shan — in Nanjing holds 350,000 plum trees across 1,500 hectares, making it one of the largest plum blossom gardens in the world. The plum blossom is Nanjing's official city flower, and the annual festival at Meihua Shan in late February and early March draws millions of visitors. The trees here range from pure white to deep rose to the prized green-calyx variety Lü'e, and during peak bloom the entire hill becomes a fragrant cloud. Walk the paths. Climb to the top for the view over the Purple Mountain area and toward the city. The plum — mei — is one of the Four Gentlemen of Chinese painting and a symbol of resilience: it flowers before winter is done, while frost still forms at night. Chinese poets from Su Shi to Lu You wrote about the plum for over a thousand years. Combine with a visit to the Ming Xiaoling Mausoleum and the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum on the same mountain. Eat a bowl of Nanjing salted duck noodles. Have tea at one of the teahouses on the hill. The plum blossoms are gentle and sparse compared to cherries — you come for the fragrance, the single perfect flower on a dark branch, and the long-cultivated silence of Chinese garden poetry.

variety: Yellow rapeseed fields against volcanic landscape and sea
tip: Climb Seongsan Ilchulbong (Sunrise Peak) at dawn for the canola fields against the crater and ocean.
story: Jeju Island is South Korea's honeymoon island and its volcanic wonder — Mount Halla rising in the center, black lava coastlines, hallabong oranges growing in small family orchards. In April, the canola fields come into bloom. Whole fields of bright yellow rapeseed blanket the volcanic slopes, against a backdrop of the deep blue sea and the occasional black basalt wall or traditional stone dol hareubang statue. The most famous canola spot is at Seongsan Ilchulbong — the Sunrise Peak — a crater jutting into the ocean on the eastern side of the island, with canola fields right up to its base. Climb the crater at sunrise for the classic view. Also visit the Gasi-ri canola road, a long driving route through continuous yellow fields. Jeju's April weather is mild and breezy, the cherry blossoms are simultaneously blooming in small villages, and the whole island takes a kind of holiday breath. Eat heukdwaeji — the local black pig, famously good — and a bowl of abalone porridge for breakfast. Drink a glass of hallasan soju. The island is small, easy to drive, and its canola season is brief but generous. Get there early, or drive twenty minutes off the tourist map for fields of pure gold with no one else in them.

variety: Desert sand verbena, lilies, primrose, sunflowers — superbloom years only
tip: Call the park's wildflower hotline before you go. Henderson Canyon Road and Coyote Canyon have the best displays.
story: Anza-Borrego Desert State Park is the largest state park in California — 600,000 acres of desert in the southern Colorado Desert — and in good rain years it produces one of the great wildflower superblooms of North America. In February and March, after a wet winter, the flat desert floor, the sloping alluvial fans, and the narrow washes fill with desert sand verbena, desert lilies, dune evening primrose, chuparosa, desert sunflowers, and the Borrego Palm Canyon's own unique flora. The park has a real-time wildflower hotline — call it before you go. Base yourself in the small town of Borrego Springs. Drive the back roads at dawn. Walk Henderson Canyon Road for sheets of purple sand verbena, and Coyote Canyon Road for the best desert lilies. Anza-Borrego does not do superblooms every year — it takes a particular sequence of autumn and winter rains — but when it happens, the desert becomes a watercolor you wouldn't have thought possible. The stars here at night are unbelievable; Anza-Borrego is an official Dark Sky Park. Eat a date shake at Shields Date Garden in nearby Indio. Go to Salvation Mountain. The Colorado Desert is one of the quieter, less-visited corners of the American West, and its flower years make it unforgettable.

variety: Magnolia grandiflora — dinner-plate blossoms, lemon fragrance
tip: Walk Forsyth Park at dusk when the magnolia scent is strongest. Combine with the historic squares north of the park.
story: Forsyth Park sits in the heart of Savannah's historic district, 30 acres of Spanish moss-draped live oaks and grand old magnolias. The Southern magnolia — Magnolia grandiflora — blooms in late spring, with cream-white flowers the size of dinner plates that release a lemony, heavy perfume across the whole park. The white marble fountain at the park's center, modeled on the Place de la Concorde in Paris, reflects flowering trees and walkers moving slowly through the heat. Magnolias are the iconic tree of the American South, and Savannah wears them with full ceremony. Combine a visit with a walking tour of the historic squares — Savannah has 22 of them, each a pocket park surrounded by 19th-century architecture — and a cup of sweet tea on a shaded porch somewhere. Stop at the Gryphon Tea Room or Leopold's ice cream. Eat shrimp and grits at a small restaurant tucked into an alley. The magnolia blooms from April through June, with peak in May. Savannah's spring has an almost impossible density of flowering trees — wisteria on wrought-iron balconies, dogwoods under the oaks, azaleas everywhere — but the magnolia is the one that signals, perfume first, that summer is on its way. Pack a book. Find a bench. Sit a while.

variety: 1,100+ orchid species including Guarianthe skinneri (Costa Rican national flower)
tip: Take the 1-hour guided tour — the smallest orchids are the ones you'd otherwise walk past.
story: The Lankester Botanical Garden outside Cartago, Costa Rica, holds one of the world's most important orchid collections — over 1,100 species, many of them native to Costa Rica's cloud forests. The garden was founded in 1917 by British botanist Charles Lankester, who came to Costa Rica to grow coffee and ended up falling in love with the country's wild orchids. The garden is small compared to other botanical gardens, but it's incredibly dense — every tree is hung with orchids, every walkway lined with them. The peak bloom is from February through May, the Costa Rican dry season, when the Guaria Morada (the country's national orchid, Guarianthe skinneri) bursts into purple clusters. Go on a weekday morning. A guided tour, even a short one, teaches you to look for orchids you would otherwise miss — tiny blooms the size of a fingernail, moth-shaped, bee-shaped, impossibly detailed. Combine with a visit to the Cartago basilica and a morning of coffee at one of the nearby fincas. Costa Rica's orchid culture goes deep — nearly 1,400 orchid species grow in the country, and many Costa Rican homes have a small plant on a porch or balcony. The Lankester garden is where you understand just how much life is folded into such tiny flowers.

variety: Handroanthus impetiginosus — purple clusters on bare branches
tip: Sunday morning at Ibirapuera is the best time — the elevated Minhocão is also pedestrianized on weekends for long views of ipês across the city.
story: In July and August, parts of São Paulo turn deep purple. The ipê roxo — Handroanthus impetiginosus, the purple trumpet tree — flowers in the coldest, driest weeks of the Brazilian winter, when the tree has dropped its leaves and only the flowers remain. It's the sister species to Rio's yellow ipê but appears in different colors and different months. The Ibirapuera Park in southern São Paulo has rows of ipês — purple, yellow, pink, and white varieties — and in late July the park becomes a patchwork of flowering tree canopies. The Avenida Paulista also has scattered ipês, and the elevated Minhocão, pedestrianized on weekends, offers long views over purple and yellow crowns along the surrounding streets. The ipê is the national tree of Brazil. Its wood is famously hard — some of the oldest railway ties in Brazil were made of ipê and still survive. The flowers appear in huge trumpet clusters on bare branches, then fall in showers of color. São Paulo's winter is cool and often gray; the ipê is the city's antidote. Have a coxinha and an espresso at a padaria. Walk Ibirapuera on a Sunday morning with the locals. The ipê gives São Paulo, briefly, the look of a watercolor painting laid over a great industrial city.

variety: Helianthus annuus — tournesols alongside the lavender rotation
tip: Drive the D6 between Valensole and Manosque in mid-July — you'll often see lavender and sunflowers both in the same view.
story: The Valensole Plateau is famous for lavender, but in mid-July — sometimes into early August — the same fields that held lavender a few weeks before come into sunflower bloom. The Provençal farmers rotate crops, and for a few weeks you can see both: ribbons of dark purple still lingering in some fields, and shoulder-high sunflowers waving gold in others, against the same sky and the same distant limestone hills. The road between Valensole and Manosque passes the best concentration. Pull over at any of the marked stopping points. Fields of sunflowers — tournesols — track the sun through the morning and turn east at evening. The combination of lavender and sunflower is what makes Valensole in late July so specific — two of the great Provençal flowers overlapping briefly. The light here is the light that painters have been drawn to for two centuries — thick, warm, golden. Eat a long lunch at a village bistro. Try the local honey, now perfumed with both flowers. Drink a glass of rosé from a Provençal vineyard. Visit the lavender distillery if it's still open. The plateau has a gentle, agricultural calm — working farmland that happens to be beautiful — and its summer colors make a case for slow travel through southern France.

variety: Crocus sativus — Greek saffron with protected designation of origin
tip: Visit during harvest at dawn — local families allow guests to join the picking. The Saffron Cooperative in Krokos has tours.
story: Saffron is the world's most expensive spice, and one of its great growing regions is Kozani in northern Greece. Here, in the foothills of the Pindus Mountains, the Crocus sativus has been cultivated for over three hundred years. The fields are small — each farmer tends a fraction of a hectare — and the flowers bloom for only two or three weeks in October and November, in bands of soft purple across the autumn landscape. The harvest is entirely by hand. Local families gather before dawn, pick the flowers one by one, and spend the afternoon plucking the three dark red stigmas from each flower — the threads that become saffron. An ancient, precise, utterly manual craft. Visit Krokos, the village at the heart of the region, during harvest season. The Saffron Cooperative offers tours of the drying rooms and a tasting of saffron-infused liqueurs, sweets, and teas. Buy a small package — Greek krokos Kozanis has a protected designation of origin and is considered among the finest in the world. Combine with a visit to Prespa Lakes, a quiet natural area on the borders of Greece, Albania, and North Macedonia. Eat Greek mountain food — tsipouro, fresh cheese, grilled meat — in a village tavern. The saffron of Kozani takes about 80,000 flowers to make a pound.

variety: 120,000 tulips — 300+ varieties arranged along Lake Geneva
tip: Combine with a walk along the lakefront promenade to the Château de Morges. On a clear day you can see Mont Blanc across the lake.
story: The small Swiss town of Morges sits on the north shore of Lake Geneva, about twenty minutes from Lausanne, and every spring its Parc de l'Indépendance fills with 120,000 tulips of every color, arranged in elegant beds along the lakefront. The annual Tulip Festival — Fête de la Tulipe — runs from late March through early May, and the park becomes one of the most photogenic spots in western Switzerland: tulips in orderly Swiss rows, Lake Geneva behind, the French Alps on the far shore across the water. Morges itself is a small lakeside town with a castle, a medieval old town, and cafés along the promenade. Walk the park, then walk the waterfront to the Château de Morges. Stop for a glass of Chasselas, the local white wine, at one of the cafés facing the lake. The Swiss take tulips as a quieter affair than the Dutch — smaller scale, neater, framed by mountains and still water rather than vast flat polder. In April, cherry blossoms also flower in the town, and on a clear day you can see Mont Blanc on the horizon. Take the slow train along the lake. This is Switzerland at its soft-spring best — neat, elegant, and almost too beautiful to be true.

variety: Jacaranda mimosifolia — purple canopy across the northern suburbs
tip: Drive the leafy streets of Highlands and Borrowdale for the most dramatic jacaranda tunnels.
story: Harare is known as the Sunshine City, and every September and October its streets fill with jacaranda blossoms. Zimbabwe's capital was designed as a garden city in the early 20th century, and the planners planted jacaranda trees — and golden-yellow cassia trees — along the wide avenues. In spring, the city becomes a pattern of purple and gold. The leafy northern suburbs — Highlands, Borrowdale — are the most dramatic, with whole residential streets turning purple. Josiah Tongogara Avenue and Sam Nujoma Street in the city center are also classic jacaranda streets. The petals fall in a continuous drift, and for weeks the pavements and gutters are lined with purple. Combine with a visit to the Harare Botanic Gardens — small, well-maintained, with indigenous Zimbabwean flora — and a drive out to Lake Chivero for a weekend. Eat sadza and beef stew at a local place. The city's music scene is strong if you know where to look, with jazz nights at a handful of old cafés. The jacaranda is not native to Zimbabwe — it came from Argentina — but it has been naturalized here for nearly a century, and Zimbabweans love it deeply. The spring purple in Harare is one of those small civic pleasures that quietly defines a city.

variety: Adenium obesum socotranum — bottle-trunked endemic with pink-white trumpets
tip: Check current travel advisories carefully. When accessible, Socotra's Haggier Plateau and Dixam Plateau have the densest desert rose populations.
story: Socotra is an island in the Arabian Sea — officially part of Yemen but geographically and biologically its own world, sometimes called the most alien-looking place on Earth. A third of its plant species grow nowhere else. The Socotran desert rose — Adenium obesum socotranum — is perhaps the most iconic: a massive, bottle-trunked tree with a huge swollen base and a tangle of silver branches, topped in February through May with pink-white flowers like small trumpets. They grow on the limestone plateaus of the Haggier Mountains and in dry valleys, alongside the dragon's blood trees with their upside-down umbrella canopies, and the cucumber trees that look like giant pale bottles. Travel to Socotra has been complicated in recent years — the political situation in Yemen has fluctuated, and charter flights from the UAE are typically the only way in. Check current advisories carefully before planning. If you do reach Socotra, you'll find yourself on beaches without another footprint, on plateaus of plants that look designed by imagination itself, in villages where Bedouin families still speak their ancient Socotri language. The desert rose blooming on red rock with the Arabian Sea below is a landscape that belongs to no easy category. It is one of the last truly strange places a traveler can go.

variety: Adansonia grandidieri — night-blooming white flowers high in ancient crowns
tip: Go for sunset, stay for the stars. The flowers open after dark in late November. Walk a kilometer in either direction from the main avenue for baobabs to yourself.
story: The Avenue of the Baobabs on the western coast of Madagascar is a short stretch of dirt road between the town of Morondava and the village of Belo sur Tsiribihina, lined with about twenty Grandidier's baobab trees — Adansonia grandidieri — that are up to eight hundred years old. The trees are enormous, gray, and seem to have their branches upside down, like roots reaching for the sky. A Malagasy legend says the gods were so annoyed by the baobab's complaints that they replanted it upside down. The baobab flowers are less well-known than the trees themselves — they bloom at night in late November and December, large and white, pollinated by fruit bats, and they wilt by noon the next day. If you're on the Avenue after sunset during flowering season, you can sometimes see the flowers opening in the fading light — massive white blooms, vaguely lotus-like, high above you in the crowns of impossibly old trees. Go for sunset, stay for the stars. The avenue is one of the most photographed places in Africa, but walk a kilometer in either direction and you'll often have baobabs to yourself. Eat koba, the sweet banana-rice cake of the region. Sleep in a small Morondava guesthouse. Madagascar's isolation has given it a flora that exists nowhere else. The baobabs are the keepers of that specificity.
